title: Austin Powers: International Man of Mystery
logline: Mike Myers as a swinging 1960s spy thawed out in the 1990s. Spy parody built on innuendo and running gags.
overview: As a swinging fashion photographer by day and a groovy British superagent by night, Austin Powers is the '60s' most shagadelic spy. But can he stop megalomaniac Dr. Evil after the bald villain freezes himself and unthaws in the '90s? With the help of sexy sidekick Vanessa Kensington, he just might.

jokes.text: When Mr. Bigglesworth gets upset... people die!
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is giving a menacing villain speech about being surrounded by assassins who have failed him; he invokes his cat's emotional state as a harbinger of death
jokes.punchline: The grandiose threat is that a fluffy cat's feelings are the trigger for mass murder — absurd logic delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Dr. Evil establishment joke — the juxtaposition of Bond-villain gravitas with a cat's feelings as the ultimate threat is perfectly calibrated. The escalating structure (Evil angry → Bigglesworth upset → people die) mimics the rhythm of genuine menace and then yanks the rug. Character-specific and highly quotable.

jokes.text: Why must I be surrounded by frickin' idiots?
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has just delivered a dramatic speech; this line comes after a beat, as a tonal deflation
jokes.punchline: The word 'frickin'' — a mock-profanity that reveals Dr. Evil is simultaneously trying to be menacing and weirdly sanitized
jokes.explanation: The 'frickin'' substitute is a small but telling character detail — Dr. Evil can't quite commit to actual profanity, which is funnier than if he just swore. Economy is excellent; the whole joke lives in one word choice.

jokes.text: Oh, behave. / Yeah, baby! / It's Austin Powers!
jokes.setup: We cut from Dr. Evil's menacing underground lair to a photo shoot; we hear Austin's catchphrases before we see him
jokes.punchline: The reveal that the voice behind these groovy catchphrases is Austin Powers — a tonal 180 from the villain scene
jokes.explanation: The first Austin Powers entrance is a character establishment joke done well. His catchphrases arrive before his face, letting the audience meet his personality before his looks. 'Oh, behave' and 'Yeah, baby' are introduced here as signature lines that will pay off throughout the film.

jokes.text: Why don't you ever model for me? / You know how Mr. Kensington feels about that.
jokes.setup: Austin flirts with his partner Mrs. Kensington at what appears to be a professional spy setting
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Kensington deflects with a reference to her husband's feelings — she's a married woman and Austin is undeterred
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for Austin's character as a shameless flirt. The joke is mild — it's more exposition than comedy — but the dynamic between Austin's relentless flirting and a sensible woman's refusal is the engine the film runs on.

jokes.text: The Electric Psychedelic Pussycat Swinger's Club here in swinging London
jokes.setup: Basil Exposition delivers a straight spy-briefing, naming the target location
jokes.punchline: The name 'Electric Psychedelic Pussycat Swinger's Club' is maximally on-the-nose 60s pastiche, delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: The character name 'Basil Exposition' (a meta-joke in itself) delivering a ridiculous club name with a straight face is a solid bit of parody writing. The joke is in the commitment to the absurd naming convention.

jokes.text: Character named 'Basil Exposition' giving the spy briefing
jokes.setup: A supporting character delivers plot-critical information in spy-movie fashion
jokes.punchline: His name is literally 'Basil Exposition' — the film names the narrative device it's using
jokes.explanation: A legitimately clever piece of meta-comedy writing. Naming the exposition character 'Basil Exposition' acknowledges the spy-movie convention it's exploiting while also making it funnier every time he appears. It's economical (the joke is entirely in the name), original in its directness, and perfectly integrated — only this character could carry this joke. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor for wit and economy.

jokes.text: Austin hits a woman at the party; reveals 'That ain't no woman. It's a man, man.'
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts with horror as Austin inexplicably punches a woman at the swinger's club
jokes.punchline: He reveals the 'woman' is a cross-dressed male assassin — Austin's intuition was correct all along
jokes.explanation: A classic spy-parody beat — Austin acts like a brute but is vindicated. 'It's a man, man' is a good piece of wordplay. The structure is solid misdirection but the concept is fairly familiar.

jokes.text: Come, Mr. Bigglesworth! / See you in the future, Mr. Powers.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is cornered and about to be captured
jokes.punchline: He dramatically scoops up his cat and delivers a Bond-villain farewell before freezing himself — the cat is his priority in an escape
jokes.explanation: The callback to Mr. Bigglesworth pays off the opening setup. Dr. Evil's priorities (cat first, menacing exit line second) are perfect character comedy. The Bond-parody 'See you in the future' is a nice touch.

jokes.text: It appears to be in the shape of a Big Boy. / Good God. He's back. / In many ways, the Big Boy never left, sir.
jokes.setup: Military radar operators speak in urgent tones about an unidentified craft with 'erratic vectoring' approaching US airspace — classic thriller framing
jokes.punchline: The ominous shape is a Big Boy restaurant mascot spaceship; then the sub-punchline: a straight officer sincerely defends Big Boy's value proposition
jokes.explanation: The layered joke structure here is excellent: (1) parody of military tension-speak, (2) absurd reveal of a fast-food mascot as the UFO, (3) the officer's sincere defense of Big Boy's prices as a straight-man non-sequitur. Three distinct laughs in quick succession. The 'Shut up' deflation is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Prepare the jet, bring my overnight bag, and feed my fish. Not too much.
jokes.setup: Commander Gilmour is reacting to a potential global crisis involving Dr. Evil's return — a situation of maximum urgency
jokes.punchline: He calmly adds mundane domestic instructions (fish feeding, with specific portion guidance) to his emergency orders
jokes.explanation: Classic bathos — the mundane inserted into the epic. 'Not too much' is the key detail that elevates it from generic to specific. The specificity of fish-feeding instructions during a global emergency is funnier than a more generic mundane detail would be.

jokes.text: We don't want to have to bail you out again like after WW II.
jokes.setup: American and British officials discuss whether Austin Powers is up to the mission
jokes.punchline: The American casually references having 'bailed out' Britain in WWII — a nationalistic jab delivered with friendly condescension
jokes.explanation: A quick political jab that gets a mild laugh. Functional but not particularly clever — it's a familiar joke about Anglo-American relations that doesn't add a fresh twist.

jokes.text: Stage five: evacuation beginning. [long pause] Evacuation comp--
jokes.setup: The clinical unfreezing stages have been announced one by one; 'evacuation' sounds medical but the interrupted announcement suggests something has gone wrong
jokes.punchline: The announcement is cut off, implying Austin's bowel evacuation after 30 years of freezing has overwhelmed the technician — the visual gag of what's happening is left to the audience's imagination (and confirmed by the interrupted line)
jokes.explanation: The interrupted announcement is an excellent piece of comedic restraint — the film doesn't show us what's happening, which makes it funnier. The buildup of the previous stages makes the payoff land harder. The 'Evacuation comp--' cut-off is a great use of the running gag structure.

jokes.text: The shouting is a temporary side effect of the unfreezing process. / Yes. I'm having difficulty controlling the volume of my voice!
jokes.setup: Basil explains that Austin will shout as a side effect — he delivers this calmly
jokes.punchline: Austin immediately demonstrates this at full volume, confirming the diagnosis with perfect comic timing
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural setup-punchline — the explanation and the demonstration happen simultaneously, so the audience gets the joke the instant Basil finishes his sentence. Well-timed and clean. The all-caps confirmation is a nice meta-visual element in the transcript.

jokes.text: Finally, those capitalist pigs will pay for their crimes. Eh, comrades? / Austin, we won. / Groovy. Smashing. Yay, capitalism.
jokes.setup: Austin has been frozen since the Cold War era; upon hearing 'the cold war's over,' he instinctively sides with the wrong team
jokes.punchline: His immediate pivot to 'Yay, capitalism' upon correction reveals he has no actual ideology — just reflexive enthusiasm for whatever side wins
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke — Austin's 60s-rebel persona leads him to reflexively assume the USSR won, and his instant reversal ('Groovy. Smashing. Yay, capitalism.') is perfectly economical. 'Yay, capitalism' is a legitimately quotable line that captures Austin's shallowness beautifully. The escalating list structure (Groovy / Smashing / Yay capitalism) is well-crafted.

jokes.text: My God, Vanessa's got a fabulous body and I bet she shags like a minx.
jokes.setup: Austin has just met Vanessa, his new partner, in a formal Ministry of Defense briefing room
jokes.punchline: He delivers his private inner thoughts about her body and sex life out loud in front of everyone
jokes.explanation: The setup for the 'no inner monologue' joke that follows. Works on its own as Austin establishing his complete lack of professional decorum, but the real craft is in how it sets up joke #18.

jokes.text: How do I tell them that because of the unfreezing process I have no inner monologue? / I hope I didn't say that out loud just now.
jokes.setup: Austin has just said something embarrassing out loud; he then wonders aloud how to explain his lack of inner monologue
jokes.punchline: His explanation of having no inner monologue is itself delivered out loud, demonstrated in real time — then 'I hope I didn't say that out loud' as a perfect button
jokes.explanation: This is one of the reel's best-constructed jokes. The structure is a triple layer: (1) Austin says something inappropriate, (2) he narrates his own problem out loud while trying to privately figure out how to explain it, (3) the button 'I hope I didn't say that out loud' confirms he still doesn't realize it. The joke demonstrates the problem through its own structure — the form IS the content. This approaches the 8.0 anchor in structural craft.

jokes.text: No doubt, luv, but as long as people are still having promiscuous sex with many anonymous partners without protection while experimenting with mind-expanding drugs in a consequence-free environment, I'll be sound as a pound.
jokes.setup: Vanessa tells Austin that a lot has changed since 1967 and he needs to acclimate to the 90s
jokes.punchline: Austin's confident response is a comprehensive checklist of exactly the behaviors that have NOT been socially acceptable since the 60s — AIDS, the war on drugs, etc. — delivered with zero awareness
jokes.explanation: A dense, well-structured joke that packs the entire fish-out-of-water premise into one sentence. The escalating list (promiscuous sex → anonymous partners → no protection → mind-expanding drugs → consequence-free) is funny because each addition makes it worse, and 'sound as a pound' as the breezy conclusion nails the character's obliviousness. Strong character integration — this only works from Austin.

jokes.text: Danger's my middle name. / Austin Danger Powers.
jokes.setup: Official reads 'Name: Danger Powers' from the form, Austin corrects him — 'my name is Austin Powers'
jokes.punchline: His middle name is literally 'Danger' — a parody of spy-movie protagonist naming conventions, and the official recites the full name with perfect deadpan
jokes.explanation: A quick, clean bit that parodies action hero naming while giving Austin an absurd full name that is actually a perfect character joke. 'Austin Danger Powers' achieves maximum ridiculousness with three words. The misdirection (correcting the form, then the correction revealing something sillier) is well-structured.

jokes.text: One Swedish-made penis enlarger pump.
jokes.setup: An official is methodically reading Austin's personal effects in a formal inventory setting — a blue suit, a cravat, a medallion
jokes.punchline: The list includes a penis enlarger pump, delivered in the same flat bureaucratic tone as everything else
jokes.explanation: The joke setup is in the bureaucratic deadpan — formal inventory reading is the perfect context for the absurd item reveal. The escalation that follows (credit card receipt, warranty card, book) makes this the first beat of a multi-part running gag.

jokes.text: That's not mine. / One credit card receipt for Swedish-made penis enlarger, signed by Austin Powers. / I'm telling you, baby, that's not mine.
jokes.setup: Austin denies ownership of the pump
jokes.punchline: The credit card receipt bearing his name immediately contradicts him
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is working well here — the denial made the credit card receipt funnier. Austin's repeated 'I'm telling you, baby, that's not mine' despite mounting evidence is a classic comic refusal-to-accept-reality bit.

jokes.text: One warranty card for Swedish-made penis enlarger pump, filled out by Austin Powers.
jokes.setup: Austin has denied the pump and the receipt; the official continues the inventory
jokes.punchline: He also filled out the warranty card — which requires extra effort and is something only a committed owner would do
jokes.explanation: The warranty card detail is funnier than the receipt because filling out warranty cards requires deliberate effort — it's a small but telling escalation that reveals a deeper level of commitment to the denied item.

jokes.text: One warranty card for Swedish-made penis enlarger pump, filled out by Austin Powers.
jokes.setup: Austin has denied both the pump and the receipt
jokes.punchline: He also filled out and returned the warranty card — an act that implies not only ownership but careful consumer behavior about the item
jokes.explanation: The warranty card beat is the comedic peak of the first two escalations — it's not just proof of purchase, it's proof of responsible consumer stewardship. Austin cared enough to send in his warranty card. This specific detail is funnier than the receipt because of its implied earnestness. 'I don't even know what this is' as Austin's response pushes credulity hilariously.

jokes.text: One book: Swedish-made Penis Enlarger Pumps And Me (This sort of thing is my bag, baby) by Austin Powers.
jokes.setup: Austin has denied the pump, the receipt, and the warranty card; the inventory continues
jokes.punchline: He not only used it — he wrote a book about it, with a subtitle that directly contradicts his repeated denials
jokes.explanation: The perfect escalation payoff. Each step (deny pump → deny receipt → deny warranty card) has been building to this. The subtitle '(This sort of thing is my bag, baby)' is the masterstroke — it uses Austin's own catchphrase against him, the parenthetical format perfectly mimics real subtitle conventions, and it ends his denials definitively while being maximally quotable. This is legitimately exceptional comedy writing — the structure builds perfectly and the payoff exceeds expectations at each beat. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor for structure; the subtitle twist pushes it higher.

jokes.text: Just sign the form. / Don't get heavy, man. I'll sign it, just to get things moving.
jokes.setup: Austin has been caught with overwhelming evidence of penis pump ownership; technician asks him to just sign the form acknowledging his effects
jokes.punchline: Austin's response — 'Don't get heavy, man. I'll sign it, just to get things moving' — is the capitulation of a man who knows he's lost but can't bring himself to admit it; 'getting things moving' as if he's doing everyone a favor
jokes.explanation: Good button on the running gag — Austin's pseudo-magnanimous signing ('just to get things moving') is a perfect character note. He's not admitting guilt; he's doing a favor. Period slang 'Don't get heavy' is authentic Austin-speak.

jokes.text: stop calling me baby. You can address me as... Agent Kensington. / Oh, come on. All right, then... Vanessa. / Was that so hard?
jokes.setup: Vanessa establishes professional boundaries and insists on being called 'Agent Kensington'
jokes.punchline: Austin negotiates it down to 'Vanessa' — refusing the professional title but compromising — and her 'Was that so hard?' treats him like a child
jokes.explanation: Functional dynamic-establishment comedy. The negotiation from 'Agent Kensington' to 'Vanessa' shows Austin's charm working partially but not fully. 'Was that so hard?' is a matronly put-down that characterizes Vanessa well.

jokes.text: Mr. Bigglesworth reveal — the cat is now completely hairless after unfreezing complications
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has mentioned Mr. Bigglesworth multiple times as his beloved fluffy cat; the unfreezing process had 'feline complications'
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Mr. Bigglesworth is now a bald hairless cat — a visual gag that pays off the multiple Bigglesworth mentions
jokes.explanation: A legitimately great visual reveal. The film has been building Bigglesworth as Dr. Evil's precious cat; the unfreezing complications are mentioned ominously; then the reveal is a completely bald Sphynx cat that Dr. Evil now cradles with the same devotion. The visual of Dr. Evil stroking a hairless cat while maintaining villainy is iconic — it's a parody of the Bond-villain trope (Blofeld's cat) taken to its logical extreme. The payoff exceeds setup expectations and is one of the film's most memorable images.

jokes.text: Somebody help me! I'm still alive, only I'm very badly burned.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is addressing his new henchmen with a formal introduction; there is a device in the room that dropped Mustafa into a pit of fire for failing with Mr. Bigglesworth
jokes.punchline: From the pit, a badly burned Mustafa interrupts the formal meeting to ask for help — entirely ignored by everyone
jokes.explanation: Dark comedy done well — the horror of Mustafa being burned alive is treated as a minor inconvenience to the meeting agenda. His polite interruptions ('Could someone call an ambulance? I'm in quite a lot of pain') contrast perfectly with the formal corporate meeting tone. The understatement of 'quite a lot of pain' is excellent.

jokes.text: Some of you I know, some of you I'm meeting for the first time. / Hello up there! Anyone! Could someone call an ambulance? I'm in quite a lot of pain.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues his formal introduction speech; Mustafa continues to interrupt from the pit
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of corporate pleasantries ('some of you I'm meeting for the first time') with a burning man's cries for help — both delivered in equally matter-of-fact tones
jokes.explanation: The parallel conversation structure — formal meeting proceeding simultaneously with burned man's cries — is the kind of sustained comedy the film does well. Mustafa's escalating specificity ('I designed this device myself — Good. I'm glad you found me.') adds a layer.

jokes.text: He's down there. No, not dead — burned. Badly.
jokes.setup: Mustafa has been trying to get help; someone apparently has checked on him from above
jokes.punchline: Mustafa clarifies his condition as 'burned. Badly.' — the specificity and the matter-of-fact tone while severely injured amplifies the dark comedy
jokes.explanation: The clarification 'No, not dead — burned. Badly.' is tight and dark. The two-word sentence 'Burned. Badly.' is well-timed economy. Each beat of Mustafa's ignored pleas escalates the dark comedy.

jokes.text: You shot me! / Moving on— / You shot me right in the arm!
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil's guards have apparently shot Mustafa when they 'found' him in the pit
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil dismisses the fact that he just had his henchman shot with 'Moving on' — Mustafa's indignant specificity ('right in the arm!') and Dr. Evil's total indifference are the joke
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the Mustafa sequence is the best one. 'Moving on' as a response to shooting someone in the arm is perfect character work for Dr. Evil — his total indifference to human suffering treated as a minor procedural matter. Mustafa's indignant specificity ('right in the arm!') is a great reaction. The escalation from burns to being shot while trying to escape is a well-structured dark comedy sequence.

jokes.text: Frau Farbissina — founder of the militant wing of the Salvation Army.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is introducing his villainous associates
jokes.punchline: Frau Farbissina's biography is 'founder of the militant wing of the Salvation Army' — a perfectly absurd combination of an inherently benevolent organization and paramilitary violence
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — eight words that contain a complete comedic concept. The 'militant wing of the Salvation Army' is funny because the Salvation Army is specifically non-militant, so its militant wing is an oxymoron that implies Frau's radicalism is so extreme she turned charity workers into fighters. High originality for such a compressed joke.

jokes.text: Random Task — Korean ex-wrestler, evil handyman extraordinaire. / Show them what you do.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil introduces an imposing henchman as an 'evil handyman extraordinaire' — the audience expects something threatening
jokes.punchline: Random Task removes his shoe and throws it — a parody of Oddjob from Goldfinger, whose deadly weapon was his razor-edged hat, here reduced to a shoe
jokes.explanation: A smart parody of the Goldfinger/Oddjob trope — a nearly identical setup with a ridiculous downgrade (hat → shoe). 'Random Task' as a name is itself a joke (Random Task = Odd Job). The visual reveal of the shoe throw presumably gets a laugh from audiences who catch the reference, and even those who don't find it absurd on its own terms.

jokes.text: They're always after me lucky charms! / Why does everyone always laugh when I say that?
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil explains that Patty O'Brien leaves Lucky Charms cereal pieces on victims — 'Scotland Yard would love to get their hands on that piece of evidence'
jokes.punchline: O'Brien indignantly says 'They're always after me lucky charms!' — which is the Lucky Charms cereal slogan — and then is baffled that people laugh, requiring a full explanation of the commercial
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: (1) an Irish assassin accidentally quoting the Lucky Charms cereal slogan, and (2) his frustrated non-awareness that it's funny, leading to an overly earnest explanation of the commercial. The extended explanation of the Lucky Charms ad ('these tiny bits of marshmallows...so that when the kids eat them, they think Oh, this is candy') is a great piece of deadpan character work.

jokes.text: Hey, leprechaun man! Won't you give your Lucky Charms?
jokes.setup: Patty O'Brien is explaining why the Lucky Charms slogan isn't funny
jokes.punchline: Someone in the meeting room mimics the commercial's children taunting the leprechaun — confirming that yes, everyone does find it funny
jokes.explanation: The button on the Lucky Charms sequence. It lands because Patty's straight-faced explanation has been building the anticipation, and someone immediately doing exactly what he's describing is a simple but effective payoff.

jokes.text: a factory in Chicago that makes miniature models of factories. / Naturally.
jokes.setup: Number Two lists Virtucon's legitimate business holdings — cable companies, steel mills, oil refineries
jokes.punchline: The final item is a factory that makes miniature models of factories — a pointless, recursive business — and Dr. Evil's 'Naturally' treats it as self-evidently sensible
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best pure absurdist jokes. The list structure builds with plausible businesses, then ends with something completely pointless and recursive. Dr. Evil's 'Naturally' is the perfect button — his validation of the nonsensical as logical is both a character joke and a commentary on corporate opacity. Economy is exceptional: the entire joke is six words plus one. Approaches the 8.0 anchor for wit and structure.

jokes.text: Prince Charles did have an affair, he admitted it, and they are now divorced. / OK, people, you have to tell me these things. I've been frozen for 30 years.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil announces his blackmail plan — threaten to expose Prince Charles's affair
jokes.punchline: His plan has already happened in reality; Number Two informs him; Dr. Evil's response treats this as a procedural oversight by his staff rather than a fundamental flaw in his plan
jokes.explanation: Excellent fish-out-of-water joke that also satirizes both supervillain genre conventions and topical tabloid culture. 'OK, people, you have to tell me these things' is brilliantly entitled — he's mad at his staff for the world moving on without him. 'I've been frozen for 30 years. Throw me a frickin' bone here' is quotable and perfectly characterizes Dr. Evil's combination of menace and petulance. The joke structure is tight: plan → already happened → Dr. Evil's blame-shifting.

jokes.text: Throw me a frickin' bone here. I'm the boss. Need the info.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has been told his blackmail plan is obsolete
jokes.punchline: He demands his staff brief him on world events he missed — expressed as an entitled corporate manager's grievance rather than a villain's frustration
jokes.explanation: The 'frickin' callback works here — it's become a character verbal tic. 'Need the info' as a villain's complaint is funny because it sounds like a middle manager demanding a weekly briefing. The deflation of evil into corporate bureaucracy is a consistent theme that this joke serves well.

jokes.text: That also already has happened.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil presents his second plan — a laser to damage the ozone layer for ransom — delivered with great confidence
jokes.punchline: Number Two's flat four-word response: that plan is also already a reality
jokes.explanation: The running gag payoff: a second plan, also already obsolete. The economy here is exceptional — four words do the entire job of the callback. Number Two's delivery is implied to be as flat and matter-of-fact as before, which makes the repetition funnier than the original. The beat between Dr. Evil's confident plan and the flat response is perfect comedic timing.

jokes.text: Shit.
jokes.setup: Both of Dr. Evil's plans have been declared obsolete by reality
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's response to learning his second plan has also already happened is a single, resigned expletive
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic economy — one word after a long buildup. The escalation from 'frickin'' to an actual expletive is itself a micro-joke. The flatness of the delivery (implied) and the absolute resignation it conveys makes this a memorable beat. Economy score of 10: you cannot say less and convey more.

jokes.text: We hold the world ransom for... one million dollars!
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has pivoted to stealing nuclear weapons to hold the world hostage; he announces the ransom amount with enormous dramatic buildup
jokes.punchline: The amount is one million dollars — comically inadequate for a nuclear ransom, delivered as if it's an astronomical sum
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most iconic moments and arguably the best joke in this reel. The structure is flawless: enormous dramatic buildup (the pause, the finger, the revelation) delivering a laughably small number. The joke is in Dr. Evil's complete unawareness that $1 million isn't world-ransom money — it reveals his 30-year freeze perfectly. The delivery has become culturally embedded. The escalation to $100 billion immediately after (at Number Two's suggestion) makes this the setup for another great payoff. This is a 9+ moment in cultural impact.

jokes.text: Don't you think we should maybe ask for more than a million dollars? / Virtucon alone makes over $9 billion a year. / Really? That's a lot more.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has just demanded $1 million as world ransom; Number Two points out this is underwhelming given Virtucon's earnings
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's genuine surprise that $9 billion is 'a lot more' than $1 million — his cluelessness about his own financial empire
jokes.explanation: The continuation of the million-dollar joke. Dr. Evil's 'Really? That's a lot more' is a perfect extension of his obliviousness — he runs a $9 billion legitimate empire and still thinks $1 million is a lot of money. This makes him simultaneously more absurd and funnier.

jokes.text: Don't you think we should maybe ask for more than a million dollars? A million dollars isn't exactly a lot of money these days. Virtucon alone makes over $9 billion a year.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has dramatically demanded one million dollars as the world ransom
jokes.punchline: Number Two points out the obvious absurdity with straight corporate logic — the ransom is less than 0.01% of their legitimate annual revenue
jokes.explanation: Number Two's straight-man correction is essential to the joke's full payoff. '$9 billion a year' makes the million-dollar demand even more absurd in retrospect — their LEGITIMATE business vastly outearns their ransom. Good structure as a callback that deepens the original joke.

jokes.text: We hold the world ransom for... one hundred billion dollars!
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has been corrected; he recalibrates the ransom demand with the same dramatic pause and finger-pinky gesture
jokes.punchline: He overcorrects massively — going from $1 million to $100 billion — skipping all reasonable amounts in between
jokes.explanation: The perfect double payoff — the same dramatic structure as the $1 million reveal but with an absurd overcorrection. Dr. Evil's understanding of money goes from $1 million to $100 billion with no middle ground, which is both a character joke (he has no sense of scale) and a parody of villain-movie convention (the numbers are always absurd). The repeated pinky gesture (implied) makes this a visual callback too.

jokes.text: OK, then. We hold the world ransom for... one hundred billion dollars! [same dramatic pinky gesture]
jokes.setup: Number Two has pointed out $1 million is insufficient; Dr. Evil reconsiders
jokes.punchline: He simply multiplies by 100,000 and delivers the new demand with identical theatrical emphasis and pinky gesture — no nuance, no reasoning, just scaling up the same performance
jokes.explanation: The callback to the pinky gesture with a number 100,000 times larger is brilliant. The humor is in the total lack of intermediate thought — no 'maybe $50 million?' He goes directly to $100 billion with the same theatrical commitment. The repetition of the exact gesture and cadence makes it a callback that earns more than the original. The jump from 1 million to 100 billion also shows Dr. Evil has no sense of scale — he doesn't understand money at any level. Close to the original in craft; the callback escalation pushes it slightly higher.

jokes.text: When you see this jet a-rockin', don't come a-knockin', baby!
jokes.setup: Austin and Vanessa are boarding his private jet; Austin is showing it off
jokes.punchline: He delivers a sex joke about his jet using a redneck-bumper-sticker format, completely inappropriate in a professional context
jokes.explanation: Classic Austin character joke — inappropriate but enthusiastic. The 'rocking/knocking' formula is familiar but Austin's earnest delivery elevates it slightly. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Sex — yes, please!
jokes.setup: Austin is filling out Ministry of Defense release forms; the form asks for 'Sex' (meaning gender/sex designation)
jokes.punchline: Austin fills in 'yes, please' — treating the bureaucratic field as an offer
jokes.explanation: An old joke (the form-field Sex/Yes Please gag has been around forever) but executed well through Austin's specific delivery and character. The originality score is dragged down by the age of the concept, but the character integration saves it — it couldn't be more Austin.

jokes.text: That's fascinating. Why don't we go in the back and shag?
jokes.setup: Vanessa has earnestly described her Oxford education and desire to travel; Austin responds with 'That's fascinating' — appearing to be listening politely
jokes.punchline: The 'That's fascinating' was not genuine — he immediately pivots to a proposition, revealing he wasn't listening at all
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the apparent politeness of 'That's fascinating' reversed immediately by an inappropriate proposition. The structure is clean and Austin's character is well-served, but the concept is familiar.

jokes.text: That's fascinating. Why don't we go in the back and shag?
jokes.setup: Vanessa has earnestly explained her Oxford credentials and desire to travel as reasons for joining intelligence
jokes.punchline: Austin's response is a one-beat 'That's fascinating' followed immediately by a proposition — the 'fascinating' is clearly insincere and functions only as an attempted transition to his actual interest
jokes.explanation: The 'That's fascinating. Why don't we go shag?' structure is a classic Austin move — a fake conversational bridge that acknowledges her words without processing them. 'That's fascinating' as a dismissal is well-executed because it's so obviously perfunctory. The bluntness of the transition is good character comedy.

jokes.text: I've been frozen for 30 years. I've gotta see if my bits and pieces are still working.
jokes.setup: Austin has propositioned Vanessa; he's asked to explain himself
jokes.punchline: His justification — checking if his genitals still function after cryogenic freezing — is both absurd and somehow almost logical
jokes.explanation: Austin's escalating list of euphemisms for genitalia is the real joke here — 'bits and pieces,' 'wedding tackle,' 'meat and two veg,' 'twig and berries.' The British slang pile-up is funnier than the core proposition. The 'Hello, lads, you still awake?' as a direct address to his own genitals is the best beat in this sequence.

jokes.text: Do I make you horny? Randy?
jokes.setup: Austin has just been thawed out and is immediately hitting on his handler/partner Vanessa in what should be a professional context
jokes.punchline: His opening gambit is the most brazen, unapologetic sexual come-on possible — 'Do I make you horny?' delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of Austin's most iconic lines. Perfectly encapsulates his character — no shame, no filter, maximum swagger. High quotability. 'Randy' as a British slang double-meaning (aroused / a name) adds a wordplay layer. The line became a cultural touchstone for the film.

jokes.text: Austin falling over repeatedly while still partially frozen — 'Oh, turbulence! Look at that! I've gone over! Oh, I fell over again!'
jokes.setup: Austin is in the middle of propositioning Vanessa but is still physically uncoordinated from the unfreezing process
jokes.punchline: He keeps toppling over, narrating his own falls with cheerful British optimism as if they're external events happening to him
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy lands because Austin narrates his own incompetence with zero self-awareness — 'I've gone over!' as if it's a weather event. The character integration is strong: only Austin would stay in seduction mode while falling over.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil's minion explaining that after a couple of years they 'got a little impatient' waiting for Dr. Evil to return — implying they used his frozen semen without him
jokes.setup: The minion explains the sentimental backstory of freezing Dr. Evil's semen just in case he didn't come back
jokes.punchline: 'After a couple of years, we got a little impatient' — delivered with bureaucratic casualness about an extremely weird decision
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery of 'we got a little impatient' perfectly captures the absurdity of the situation — these evil henchmen couldn't wait a few more years to use their boss's frozen semen. The understatement does heavy lifting.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil meeting his son Scott for the first time — 'I'm your father.' Long awkward pause.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is introduced to the son he's never met, delivering the line 'I'm your father' with apparent dramatic sincerity
jokes.punchline: The long beat of silence from Scott, visually communicating complete contempt — the absence of the expected emotional reunion
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm your father' line is a Star Wars parody with added absurdist weight — delivered by an actual supervillain to a teenager who clearly despises him. The silence is funnier than any comeback Scott could give. The 8-second gap between [25:14] and [25:22] is the joke.

jokes.text: Scott Evil: 'I haven't seen you my whole life and now you come back and just expect a relationship? I hate you.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil tries to have a touching father-son moment with Scott, whom he's never met
jokes.punchline: Scott's blunt, teenage-angst 'I hate you' delivered as if this is a totally normal thing to say to your supervillain father on first meeting
jokes.explanation: Scott's character is a perfect comedic foil — a world-weary, emotionally damaged teenager as the son of a supervillain. The joke is that his grievances are entirely legitimate by normal standards but absurd in context. The character integration is strong.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil trying to get a hug from Scott — 'Could I have a hug? Give me a hug. Let's go. Pronto. I'm with it. I'm hip.' while Scott refuses and retreats
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil, a man of supreme power and menace, desperately tries to get his teenage son to hug him
jokes.punchline: The escalating desperation — 'Pronto. I'm with it. I'm hip.' — reveals Dr. Evil has no idea how to be a father and is using his villain command voice to request affection
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Dr. Evil's terrifying authority and his pathetic parental desperation is the richest comic vein in this reel. 'I'm with it. I'm hip.' trying to be cool to coax a hug is a perfect character detail — he applies the same imperious energy to fatherhood as to world domination and it fails completely. Near-8 territory for character integration.

jokes.text: 'Don't look at me like I'm frickin' Frankenstein. Give your father a hug.' / Scott: 'Hey, don't touch me! Get away from me, you lazy-eyed psycho!'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues pursuing Scott for a hug, now escalating to physical pursuit
jokes.punchline: Scott calls him a 'lazy-eyed psycho' — an insult that is both hilariously specific (referencing Dr. Evil's physical appearance) and perfectly captures a teenager's scorn
jokes.explanation: 'Lazy-eyed psycho' is a great insult because it's both accurate (Dr. Evil does have a distinctive look) and delivered with the total disdain only a teenager can muster. 'Frickin' Frankenstein' from Dr. Evil is also funny — he's self-pitying about not getting a hug from his own creation.

jokes.text: Austin's extended 'shall we shag' speech including 'top and tails, whore's bath' and giving his undercarriage 'a bit of a how's-your-father'
jokes.setup: Austin is supposedly accepting the sofa situation but pivots immediately back to sexual overture, now with elaborate pre-sex hygiene suggestions
jokes.punchline: The cascade of British euphemisms for sex and personal grooming, each more bizarre than the last, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: 'How's-your-father' as a euphemism for cleaning one's undercarriage is peak Austin Powers — combining British slang, sexual innuendo, and earnest personal hygiene in one sentence. Only Austin would explain his pre-sex routine unprompted. 'Whore's bath' is a great low-culture detail.

jokes.text: 'I'm just trying to get a rise out of you, for shits and giggles.'
jokes.setup: Austin backtracks, claiming his elaborate sexual advance was just a joke to get a reaction
jokes.punchline: 'Get a rise out of you' — a crude double entendre that undercuts his supposed retreat, followed by 'shits and giggles' as a casually vulgar British phrase
jokes.explanation: A solid throwaway that works because Austin's 'retreat' is itself another come-on. The double entendre of 'rise' is obvious but deployed with timing. 'Shits and giggles' has mild shock value in this context.

jokes.text: Austin unpacks his bag and a Swedish penis enlarger falls out — 'How did this get in here? Somebody's playing a prank on me. Honestly, it's not mine.'
jokes.setup: Austin is unpacking his travel bag in front of Vanessa in a supposedly professional hotel room sharing context
jokes.punchline: A Swedish penis enlarger falls out and Austin immediately denies ownership with increasingly suspicious specificity — 'somebody's playing a prank,' 'it's not mine' — while Vanessa watches
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed visual gag with a layered punchline. The object itself is funny; Austin's frantic denial makes it funnier because his protests are so specific they become more incriminating. The timing of 'honestly, it's not mine' after two prior denials is structurally sound. The visual of Vanessa's reaction (inferred) completes the joke.

jokes.text: Blimey... nerd alert!
jokes.setup: Austin opens his suitcase, which has apparently been packed with extremely nerdy or outdated/strange items.
jokes.punchline: 'Nerd alert!' delivered with surprise at his own luggage contents — the joke being either that someone packed nerd items for him or that Austin himself packed them without irony, calling them out from the outside.
jokes.explanation: A visual gag dependent on what's in the suitcase (spy gadgets, 60s paraphernalia, Swedish-made penis enlarger pump — which is paid off moments later). The 'nerd alert' is Austin's self-aware exclamation about his own gear. Transitional humor.

jokes.text: Austin hits AGAIN on 5 — 'I also like to live dangerously.' Then loses.
jokes.setup: Having already established 'I like to live dangerously' as his blackjack philosophy with a 17, Austin now has a 5 — an even more absurd context for the same motto
jokes.punchline: 'I ALSO like to live dangerously' — the 'also' perfectly signals self-awareness of the callback while still committing to the bit, then he loses
jokes.explanation: The 'also' is the key word — it acknowledges the repetition and leans into it. The escalation from hitting on 17 (bad) to hitting on 5 (absurd) with the same justification and then immediately losing is structurally tight. The running gag form here is used correctly: the callback is funnier than the original.

jokes.text: 'I won't lie to you. Cards are not my bag, baby.'
jokes.setup: Austin has just catastrophically lost at blackjack by hitting twice unnecessarily
jokes.punchline: His completely composed, underplayed admission that cards 'are not my bag' — as if he's calmly assessing a minor hobby mismatch rather than embarrassing himself at a $10,000 minimum table
jokes.explanation: 'Not my bag, baby' is very Austin — a breezy British idiom deployed with his characteristic unflappable cool. The understatement after the elaborate self-destruction at the table is well-timed.

jokes.text: Austin introduces himself: 'My name is Richie Cunningham, and this is my wife Oprah.'
jokes.setup: Austin needs to give a cover name to Number Two's group while posing as a married couple
jokes.punchline: He gives two of the most famous American names of the era — Richie Cunningham (Happy Days) and Oprah Winfrey — as if they're plausible aliases for a British man and his partner
jokes.explanation: The absurdity is well-calibrated: Richie Cunningham is an '80s TV reference used by a man from the '60s, and 'Oprah' as an alias for his white British female partner is delightfully bizarre. The names are culturally specific enough to be funny without being mere name-drops — the incongruity IS the joke.

jokes.text: 'Her name is Alotta... Alotta Fagina.'
jokes.setup: Number Two formally introduces his Italian confidential secretary
jokes.punchline: The name 'Alotta Fagina' — a Bond-girl name parody that is phonetically explicit
jokes.explanation: A Bond-name parody in the tradition of Pussy Galore and Honey Ryder. The pause between 'Alotta' and 'Fagina' (implied by delivery) is structurally important — it lets the audience anticipate before the full name lands. The name is genuinely clever as a parody: it sounds almost plausible as Italian.

jokes.text: Austin's reaction to 'Alotta Fagina' — 'Come again? I'm just not getting it. It sounded like you said your name was a lot of...'
jokes.setup: Number Two has just introduced Alotta Fagina by name
jokes.punchline: Austin plays dumb in a prolonged, juvenile way — 'Come again? I'm just not getting it' — before trailing off, refusing to actually say what he thinks he heard
jokes.explanation: The reaction joke doubles the name gag. Austin's faux confusion — 'I'm just not getting it' said in a tone that makes clear he absolutely is getting it — is a good bit of character comedy. The trailing off before saying the obvious is well-timed.

jokes.text: Come again? I'm just not getting it. It sounded like you said your name was a lot of... / Never mind.
jokes.setup: Austin has just heard the name 'Alotta Fagina' and is visibly processing it.
jokes.punchline: His drawn-out attempt to repeat back what he heard — trailing off before the word — builds comedic tension, then Number Two's flat 'Never mind' cuts it off. The audience knows exactly what Austin almost said.
jokes.explanation: The 'come again?' callback extends the name joke with good timing. 'I'm just not getting it' is a perfect line because it's simultaneously Austin not quite completing the connection and absolutely completing the connection. The trailing '...a lot of...' with the audience filling in the blank is excellent comedic economy.

jokes.text: 'What exactly do you do, Mr. Number Two?' / 'That's my business.' / 'If you'll excuse me, I have to go to the little boys' room.'
jokes.setup: Austin asks Number Two what he does, playing on his name
jokes.punchline: Number Two says 'that's my business' (meaning it's private/secret) and then immediately says he needs to go to the bathroom — 'going number two' is quite literally his business
jokes.explanation: A smart, layered pun: 'That's my business' works as a double meaning (criminal/bathroom), and then 'I have to go to the little boys' room' immediately literalizes it. The structure is clean — the setup/double meaning/literalization triple play. Well-constructed wordplay.

jokes.text: If you'll excuse me, I have to go to the little boys' room.
jokes.setup: Number Two has just said 'that's my business' in response to being asked what he does.
jokes.punchline: He immediately exits to the bathroom — the name 'Number Two' now paid off in the most literal way possible. The setup and punchline are separated by one line.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'that's my business' to 'I have to go to the little boys' room' is timed well and sets up the extended bathroom comedy scene. The whole sequence is a sustained joke about the name Number Two, and this is the moment it crystallizes. Good structural setup.

jokes.text: Cowboy at the urinal sees Austin's flamboyant outfit and says 'That is one crazy getup you got there, fella.' / Austin: 'Thank you.' / Cowboy: 'Are you in the show?' / Austin: 'No, actually, I'm English.' / Cowboy: 'I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: A regular American cowboy encounters Austin's outrageous mod outfit in the casino and assumes he must be a performer
jokes.punchline: Austin says he's just English; the cowboy's reflexive 'I'm sorry' — as if being English is itself an affliction requiring condolences
jokes.explanation: A compact national-identity joke that works on two levels: the visual comedy of Austin's outfit, and the American assumption that the only reason to dress that way is showbiz. 'I'm sorry' as a condolence for being English is a good, economical punchline. Sets up the cowboy as a character for the bathroom sequence.

jokes.text: 'Who does Number Two work for?' — Austin asks this earnestly in a bathroom stall, apparently unaware of the double meaning
jokes.setup: Austin is in the casino bathroom, apparently conducting surveillance; he asks aloud 'Who does Number Two work for?' meaning the villain
jokes.punchline: The question is a scatological double entendre — heard by a cowboy in the next stall who takes it literally and interprets it as bathroom encouragement
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The 'Who does Number Two work for?' line is a perfect double entendre that works on both levels simultaneously — Austin is completely sincere about his spy question, while the cowboy hears bathroom coaching. The structure is exceptionally tight: the setup, the audience's dawning realization, and the cowboy's response ('That's right buddy, you show that turd who's boss') all land in sequence. This is comparable to an 8+ in craft.

jokes.text: Cowboy responds: 'That's right, buddy. You show that turd who's boss.'
jokes.setup: The cowboy has heard Austin's spy question 'Who does Number Two work for?' as bathroom encouragement
jokes.punchline: 'You show that turd who's boss' — the cowboy's earnest, macho encouragement is the literalized payoff of the double meaning
jokes.explanation: 'You show that turd who's boss' is quotable in its own right and perfectly completes the double-meaning structure. The cowboy's earnest, locker-room machismo applied to defecation is a great character detail. This line became one of the film's most quoted moments.

jokes.text: Cowboy continues coaching: 'Grab ahold of something, bite your lip, and give it hell. We're gonna get through this.'
jokes.setup: The cowboy bathroom coach is now fully committed to helping Austin through his supposed bathroom struggle
jokes.punchline: 'We're gonna get through this' — the escalating gravity of the coaching, treating a bowel movement like a team sport or crisis, peaks with this absurd solidarity pledge
jokes.explanation: The escalating coaching reaches maximum absurdity with 'We're gonna get through this.' The extended commitment to the bit (across jokes 20-23) works because each beat adds something: the question, the first response, the coaching, the final disgust. This beat is the warmest and most team-spirit one.

jokes.text: 'That sounds pretty nasty. How about a courtesy flush over there?' / 'Jesus Christ, boy. What did you eat?'
jokes.setup: The bathroom scene continues; sounds (implied) have shifted the cowboy's coaching to concern and disgust
jokes.punchline: The cowboy's escalation from cheerleader to horrified bystander — 'What did you eat?' — is the final beat of the extended bathroom sequence
jokes.explanation: The final beat of the bathroom sequence where the cowboy goes from team-sport energy to genuine horror. 'What did you eat?' is a good closing line. The sequence as a whole is funnier than any individual beat, and this caps it well.

jokes.text: one million dollars! [pause] ...Sorry. One hundred billion dollars.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is making his ransom demand to the UN Security Council — the classic villain extortion scene. He builds to his demand with appropriate menace.
jokes.punchline: He demands 'one million dollars!' — a comically small amount for nuclear extortion — then catches himself and awkwardly corrects to '$100 billion.' The pause and 'Sorry' suggest he had planned a different amount and forgot to adjust for inflation.
jokes.explanation: The most iconic joke in the film and arguably one of the most quotable moments in 1990s comedy. The structure is perfect: villain theatrics build maximum expectation, then the deflation of 'one million dollars' is both a parody of outdated villainry and a character note (Dr. Evil has been frozen since the 60s). The apologetic 'Sorry' and awkward correction to $100 billion is a masterclass in comedic timing. The finger-to-lip gesture (implied) became a cultural symbol. This is a 9+ moment — genuinely comparable to iconic TV comedy moments.

jokes.text: UN rep says 'Now, Mr. Evil—' / Dr. Evil: 'Dr. Evil. I didn't spend six years in evil medical school to be called mister, thank you very much.'
jokes.setup: The UN rep addresses Dr. Evil informally as 'Mr. Evil'
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't spend six years in evil medical school to be called mister' — Dr. Evil applies the entirely normal professional grievance of a doctor demanding their title to the concept of evil medical school
jokes.explanation: A genuinely exceptional joke. The concept of 'evil medical school' as a real institution with real credentials that deserve professional respect is a perfect absurdist extension of the supervillain world. The petty dignity of insisting on 'Dr.' while holding the world hostage is a perfect character contradiction. The economy is superb — it's one sentence that unpacks an entire world. This is comfortably in the 8+ tier.

jokes.text: UN rep: 'It is the policy of the United Nations not to negotiate with terrorists.' / Dr. Evil: 'Really? So long.'
jokes.setup: The UN rep invokes standard anti-terrorist policy as a reason not to pay the ransom
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's completely casual 'Really? So long.' — he has no counter-argument and no wounded pride, he just hangs up with the energy of someone ending a disappointing phone call
jokes.explanation: Dr. Evil's immediate, unbothered 'So long' subverts the expectation of a villain's wounded rage at being rebuffed. The confidence of just hanging up — without a threat, without blustering — is a funny character choice. 'Really?' plus 'So long' is two words doing maximum work.

jokes.text: Vanessa's mother: 'In Britain in the sixties, you could be a sex symbol and still have bad teeth. It didn't matter.'
jokes.setup: Vanessa is discussing Austin's bizarre appeal with her mother on the phone; the subject of his teeth comes up
jokes.punchline: Her mother's matter-of-fact cultural observation that British '60s sex symbols were exempt from dental standards
jokes.explanation: A smart observational joke about British dental culture that doubles as character exposition. It's funny because it's delivered as cultural fact by a woman who clearly knew Austin, and it explains away the film's most obvious physical gag with historical context.

jokes.text: 'That's Dr. Evil's cat.' / 'How can you tell?' / 'I never forget a pussy...' [beat] '...cat. Oh, no. He's gone away.'
jokes.setup: Austin spots a cat in a limo and identifies it as Dr. Evil's
jokes.punchline: The deliberate pause after 'pussy' before completing the word '...cat' — Austin himself inserting the innuendo pause — followed by his mournful 'Oh, no. He's gone away.'
jokes.explanation: A reliable Austin Powers innuendo structure — the pause before '...cat' is a well-worn device but executed well here. 'He's gone away' as a lament is a good tag. The double meaning works because it's both plot-relevant (the cat) and characteristic of Austin.

jokes.text: Austin, trying to make a move on Vanessa on the dance floor, is interrupted by a Twister game — 'Right hand green!'
jokes.setup: Austin and Vanessa are dancing at the casino; Austin is making romantic moves
jokes.punchline: A Twister game appears to have broken out on the dance floor, with someone calling 'Right hand green!' — interrupting the moment with complete absurdity
jokes.explanation: A brief visual absurdism that lands as a mild gag. The incongruity of Twister on a Las Vegas dance floor is funny but underdeveloped — it's more of a sight gag that works in the moment without leaving a lasting impression.

jokes.text: Right hand green! [Austin apparently plays Twister with someone in a date context]
jokes.setup: Austin is on a date/night out with Vanessa, trying to romance her.
jokes.punchline: The date activity is apparently Twister — the most absurdly 60s/kitsch party game — framed as a romantic gesture. 'Right hand green!' delivered with full Austin enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: The visual of Austin playing Twister as courtship is funny but the transcript-only evidence is thin here. The game's inherent bodily-contact-as-innocent-game quality fits Austin's character perfectly. Transitional gag.

jokes.text: Austin's escalating series of unnecessary vehicle/route substitutions: 'Why don't I take the stairs? Why take the stairs when I could take the escalator? Why take the escalator when I've got a perfectly good canoe? I know what — I'll take the elevator.'
jokes.setup: Austin needs to get from one floor to another in a hotel/casino; he seems to be drunk or high and starts cycling through increasingly absurd travel options
jokes.punchline: The sequence escalates from sensible (stairs) to slightly better (escalator) to completely impossible (canoe) before settling on the obvious elevator — the canoe being the peak absurdity in an enclosed building
jokes.explanation: A great escalation sequence. The logic is impeccable in its absurdity — each substitution is internally consistent ('why take X when I have Y') until 'canoe' breaks it completely. The return to 'elevator' as the resolution is funny because it's what he should have done immediately. The comedic arc (sensible → escalating → impossible → obvious) is well-structured.

jokes.text: Austin trips: 'Oh, I tripped. I haven't had this much fun since college.'
jokes.setup: Austin is clearly drunk/charming on the evening out with Vanessa; he trips
jokes.punchline: 'I haven't had this much fun since college' — delivered as if tripping is an intentional pleasure and college was a golden era of falling over
jokes.explanation: A mild throwaway gag. 'I haven't had this much fun since college' is a recognizable structure but applied too generically here. Gets a small laugh but doesn't add much character or story.

jokes.text: Vanessa says 'I'm sorry.' / Austin: 'Why?' / Vanessa: 'I'm sorry that bug up your ass had to die.'
jokes.setup: Austin apologizes for something; Vanessa responds with her own 'I'm sorry'
jokes.punchline: 'I'm sorry that bug up your ass had to die' — Vanessa's acerbic comeback suggesting that Austin's loosening up means the metaphorical stick/bug has finally departed
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed comeback. 'The bug up your ass had to die' is a fresh variation on 'stick up your ass' and implies Vanessa is loosening up while simultaneously insulting her prior uptightness. Good character work for Vanessa's arc.

jokes.text: 'No, this is me in a nutshell: Help! I'm in a nutshell! How did I get into this nutshell? Look at the size of this bloody great big— What sort of shell has a nut like this?'
jokes.setup: Vanessa says Austin is 'always wanting to have fun, that's you in a nutshell'; Austin takes the metaphor literally
jokes.punchline: Austin physically enacts being trapped in a nutshell, escalating into full panic — 'How did I get into this nutshell?' — treating the idiom as a spatial emergency
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent bit. The literalization of 'in a nutshell' is a standard comedy device but Mike Myers commits to it completely, escalating from confusion to panic to geometric curiosity ('What sort of shell has a nut like this?'). The progression — trapped, confused, scientifically puzzled — shows real comedic intelligence. The character integration is strong: only Austin would engage with a metaphor this literally and with this much physical commitment. Comparable to an 8+ in craft.

jokes.text: Kiss me. / I can't, darling. You're drunk. It's not right. / I'm not drunk. / Yes, you are. / No, I'm the sensible one. I'm always the designated driver.
jokes.setup: Vanessa is apparently drunk and asking Austin to kiss her; he refuses on moral grounds.
jokes.punchline: Austin claiming to be 'the sensible one' and 'always the designated driver' — given his entire characterization as an uninhibited hedonist — is a perfect ironic reversal. Austin as the restrained moral authority is completely against type.
jokes.explanation: The role reversal — Austin as the responsible one — is funny because it's so wrong for the character. 'I'm always the designated driver' is a perfect mundane claim for a man who was frozen in cryogenic suspension. The irony of Austin restraining himself for once is well-played.

jokes.text: 'If there was one other cat in this world that could have loved her... it was me. But unfortunately for yours truly... that train has sailed.'
jokes.setup: Austin is drunkenly confessing his feelings about Vanessa's mother to a touched Vanessa
jokes.punchline: 'That train has sailed' — a perfect mixed metaphor combining 'that ship has sailed' with 'that train has left the station'
jokes.explanation: A deceptively great joke. 'That train has sailed' is a perfect malapropism/mixed metaphor that works on multiple levels: it characterizes Austin as someone whose idioms are slightly off (frozen in the '60s, possibly drunk), and the warmth of the preceding speech makes the flub land with extra affection. The economy is excellent — four words that do real comedy work while also advancing character. This is a quotable, rewatch-worthy moment.

jokes.text: 'Austin needs his hand back.' — Vanessa has fallen asleep holding Austin's hand; he has to announce it in the third person to retrieve it
jokes.setup: Vanessa has fallen asleep, apparently having grabbed Austin's hand during the tender moment; he needs it back
jokes.punchline: The formal third-person announcement 'Austin needs his hand back' — as if a PA system request would be more polite than waking her
jokes.explanation: Five words of perfect comedic economy. The third-person self-reference implies Austin has a formal relationship with his own body, and the delicacy of not wanting to wake her despite just trying to seduce her all night is a sweet character contradiction. 'Austin needs his hand back' is a great line.

jokes.text: 'What do you want... Mr. Cunningham, was it?' / Austin: 'Your boss, Number Two — I understand that cat's involved in big underground drills.' / Alotta: 'How did you know?' / Austin: 'I didn't, baby. You just told me.'
jokes.setup: Austin sneaks into Alotta Fagina's penthouse and bluffs about knowing Number Two's secret operations
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't, baby. You just told me.' — the classic spy bluff technique delivered with Austin's breezy confidence, and it actually worked
jokes.explanation: A clean spy-genre joke where Austin's incompetence accidentally produces a genuine intelligence result. 'I didn't, baby. You just told me.' is a good line — it's the right spy-movie beat delivered with Austin's specific swagger. Works both as genre parody and as Austin-specific character comedy.

jokes.text: Your boss, Number Two... I understand that cat's involved in big underground drills. / How did you know? / I didn't, baby. You just told me.
jokes.setup: Austin is pumping Alotta Fagina for information about Dr. Evil's operation, using a classic spy bluff — stating information as fact to provoke a revealing reaction.
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't, baby. You just told me.' — Austin successfully executes the spy bluff, delivering the reveal with perfect cool. For once he's genuinely competent as a spy.
jokes.explanation: The spy bluff followed by the casual reveal is a genuinely well-constructed beat. Austin competently executing a classic spy tactic is funnier in context because we've seen him be so incompetent at everything else. 'I didn't, baby. You just told me.' is delivered with genuine cool and earns the moment. Good structure.

jokes.text: 'Oh, behave.' — Austin's reaction as Alotta Fagina goes to 'slip into something more comfortable', then Austin's wide-eyed 'Good God.' as she presumably reappears
jokes.setup: Alotta says she'll slip into something more comfortable — the classic seduction cliché; Austin tries to play it cool with 'Oh, behave'
jokes.punchline: His immediate, involuntary 'Good God.' when she returns — his composure completely collapses despite the catchphrase bravado a moment before
jokes.explanation: 'Oh, behave' as a catchphrase undercut by 'Good God' is a good reaction-beat structure. Austin's self-presentation versus his actual response is a reliable character engine. The visual of what prompts 'Good God' is left to imagination (or memory from watching the film), which works well.

jokes.text: May I wash you? / Groovy, baby.
jokes.setup: Austin is in a Japanese bath house in an apparently formal, exotic setting
jokes.punchline: Austin enthusiastically agrees to being washed, treating a cultural ritual as a sexual perk, in total character
jokes.explanation: Light character beat — Austin's immediate, gleeful acceptance of being washed plays on his libido-first ethos. Functional but not special.

jokes.text: That feels yummy.
jokes.setup: Austin is being bathed/massaged in a Japanese bath house
jokes.punchline: His entirely unselfconscious, childlike word choice ('yummy') while presumably in a sensual situation deflates any sophistication
jokes.explanation: One-word gag that lands purely on the absurdity of 'yummy' as Austin's response. Character-consistent but slight.

jokes.text: In Japan, men come first, and women come second.
jokes.setup: Austin makes a seemingly earnest cultural observation about Japanese customs
jokes.punchline: The double entendre on 'come' turns a cultural remark into a sexual innuendo
jokes.explanation: Clean double-entendre setup with good delivery economy. The 'cultural observation' framing gives it just enough plausible deniability.

jokes.text: Or sometimes not at all.
jokes.setup: Previous line established the men-come-first double entendre
jokes.punchline: The tag undercuts the innuendo further by implying women don't orgasm — darker, more committed to the bit
jokes.explanation: The escalation tag is the stronger half of the two-part joke. Perfectly timed, economical to the point of being just four words, and commits to the innuendo with a darker twist. Good structure.

jokes.text: Care for some saké? / Saké it to me, baby.
jokes.setup: Attendant offers saké politely
jokes.punchline: Austin riffs on 'Sock it to me' (Laugh-In catchphrase) using the word 'saké', slathering his trademark 'baby' on top
jokes.explanation: Classic Austin wordplay — uses a 60s pop-culture pun (Laugh-In's 'Sock it to me') in a new context. The joke works because it's perfectly in character and delivers a pun that actually fits the situation. Moderate craft.

jokes.text: Kinky. / Klinky.
jokes.setup: Austin says 'Kinky' in response to something in the bath house; attendant responds 'Klinky'
jokes.punchline: The attendant mishears/mispronounces 'kinky' as 'klinky', a nonsense non-word that deflates Austin's intended innuendo
jokes.explanation: Quick, light gag — the deflation of Austin's innuendo by a linguistic misfire. Slight and forgettable.

jokes.text: How dare you break wind before me! / I'm sorry, I didn't know it was your turn.
jokes.setup: Bath attendant scolds someone for passing gas in a formal, outraged tone: 'How dare you break wind before me!'
jokes.punchline: Austin's response treats 'before me' as a question of turn order rather than a formal affront, recontextualizing the scolding as a scheduling complaint
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the outraged formal English idiom 'before me' has two meanings (in my presence vs. before my turn), and Austin takes the absurd interpretation entirely earnestly. The punchline is economical and the logical consistency of the wrong reading makes it land well. Above-average craft for this film.

jokes.text: Pardon me for being rude / It was my food / It just popped up to say hello / and now it's gone back down below. / That's beautiful. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Following the flatulence exchange, Austin recites a little rhyming poem about his fart
jokes.punchline: The attendant sincerely calls the fart poem 'beautiful,' and Austin accepts the compliment with equal sincerity — two characters treating flatulence verse as genuine art
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the previous gag to an actual recited fart poem, treated with mutual artistic appreciation, is a nice absurdist payoff. The earnestness of both parties elevates what could be pure toilet humor.

jokes.text: Let's make love, you silly hairy little man. / I say! Hello, vicar.
jokes.setup: Bath attendant proposes sex; we expect Austin to immediately agree given his established character
jokes.punchline: Austin instead spots someone off-screen and cheerfully greets a vicar, treating a sex proposition with the same casual energy as noticing a clergyman nearby — and the juxtaposition of 'vicar' and the sex invitation is itself the gag
jokes.explanation: Good subversion — the expected Austin response (immediate eager agreement) is replaced by an incongruous social greeting to a vicar. The clash between the erotic and the ecclesiastical is very British and very Austin.

jokes.text: I like to see girls of that...caliber. By caliber, of course, I mean both the size of their gun barrels and the high quality of their character. It's two meanings. Caliber — it's a homonym.
jokes.setup: Fembots have just demonstrated their lethality; Dr. Evil compliments them
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's double-entendre is so obvious he immediately explains it in full, labeling it a 'homonym' — the joke is that he can't just land a smooth line and walk away; he has to annotate it
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. The gag works on multiple levels: the double-entendre itself, the villain's inability to let it land naturally, and the pedantic linguistics lesson ('it's a homonym'). The 'Forget it' that follows seals it. This is pure Dr. Evil — his self-undermining grandiosity applied to wordplay. Character integration is near-perfect; only he would ruin his own pun this way.

jokes.text: Forget it. (Dr. Evil gives up explaining the homonym joke)
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has just laboriously explained his caliber pun to an audience that clearly didn't need or want the explanation
jokes.punchline: He abandons the explanation entirely, recognizing the moment is dead — the defeat is funnier than the explanation
jokes.explanation: The tag 'Forget it' is the capper to the caliber joke. The micro-beat of Dr. Evil recognizing his own failure and moving on is a perfect character moment. Works as a unit with joke #10.

jokes.text: Let me guess. The floss is garrote wire, the toothpaste is plastic explosives, and the toothbrush is the detonation device.
jokes.setup: Basil presents Austin with what appears to be a standard spy gadget kit; Austin confidently rattles off the spy uses for each item
jokes.punchline: Basil says 'No, actually. Since you've been frozen, there have been fabulous advances in the field of dentistry.' The spy gadgets are just... dental hygiene products.
jokes.explanation: Smart spy-genre parody — plays on the well-worn trope of Q-branch gadget reveals (Bond) and inverts it. Austin's confident listing of spy functions is immediately deflated by the mundane truth that they're just toiletries. The 'advances in dentistry' punchline is genuinely clever and subverts the genre expectation with real wit.

jokes.text: Only two things scare me, and one is nuclear war. / What's the other? / Carnies. Circus folk. Nomads, you know. Smell like cabbage. Small hands.
jokes.setup: Basil mentions Dr. Evil has hijacked a nuclear warhead — a genuinely scary proposition. Austin says only two things scare him, one being nuclear war.
jokes.punchline: The second fear is an absurdly specific, randomly phobic description of carnival workers, delivered with the same gravity as nuclear war
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The setup promises a grave, character-revealing second fear; the punchline delivers an absurdly specific, escalating list of carny grievances delivered with total sincerity ('Smell like cabbage. Small hands.'). The specificity is what makes it land — not just 'carnies' but the itemized physical complaints. Highly quotable, perfectly economical, and could only come from Austin's particular brand of confident absurdism. Craft score of 8.0 is justified by the quality of the escalating specifics.

jokes.text: Austin did some reconnaissance work last night at Alotta Fagina's penthouse.
jokes.setup: Basil is reporting straight-facedly on intelligence gathering
jokes.punchline: The name 'Alotta Fagina' is said completely straight in a formal briefing context, the absurdity heightened by Basil's total lack of reaction
jokes.explanation: The name joke has diminishing returns on repeat, but the deadpan delivery in a formal briefing context still lands. The humor is in Basil's complete composure saying 'Alotta Fagina' as though it's a perfectly normal name.

jokes.text: This is my mother — Mrs. Exposition.
jokes.setup: Basil introduces a woman to Austin
jokes.punchline: Her surname is 'Exposition' — a meta joke that the character named Basil Exposition exists solely to deliver expository information, and now his mother shares the name
jokes.explanation: Extending the running meta-joke about Basil's name. Funny to those who've been tracking it, but the laugh here is primarily recognition humor — the meta-commentary was funnier the first time it was established.

jokes.text: My God, man, what have you done? That's not your mother. It's a man, baby!
jokes.setup: Austin apparently grabs or attacks Mrs. Exposition, believing her to be a man in disguise
jokes.punchline: 'It's a man, baby!' — Austin's signature catchphrase used here in its literal application; he genuinely thinks Basil's mother is a man
jokes.explanation: One of the film's most quotable catchphrase deliveries. The craft is moderate — it's a physical misidentification gag — but the commitment and the specific phrase 'It's a man, baby!' elevated this to cultural currency. High quotability for a reason.

jokes.text: You have to admit, she is rather mannish. No offense, but if that is a woman, it does look like she was beaten with an ugly stick.
jokes.setup: Basil angrily defends his mother after Austin attacked her believing she was a man
jokes.punchline: Austin doubles down with 'mannish' and then escalates to 'beaten with an ugly stick' — not backing down at all while trying to seem reasonable
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Austin's insults while attempting diplomacy is in character — he genuinely means well while being oblivious. The 'ugly stick' phrase is old but applied with enough gusto. Functional escalation.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil and Scott in group therapy; Scott reveals his father was 'partially frozen his whole life' and that he wants Scott to 'take over the world'
jokes.setup: A family therapy session where participants share their feelings about their fathers
jokes.punchline: Scott describes his family situation in therapy-speak, but the content is supervillain life — 'partially frozen his whole life,' wants him to take over the world — delivered to a therapist treating it as normal family dysfunction
jokes.explanation: The therapy scene is a sustained comic premise — placing a supervillain and his son in group therapy and treating supervillain grievances as mundane family issues. This beat establishes the premise well. The collision of the banal (therapy) and the extreme (world domination) is the film's Dr. Evil comedy engine at its best here.

jokes.text: He comes back and wants me to take over the family business. / But, Scott, who's going to take over the world when I die?
jokes.setup: Scott is complaining about parental pressure to join the family business — a relatable teenager complaint
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's version of 'the family business' is taking over the world, stated plainly in a therapy setting
jokes.explanation: Dr. Evil's earnest, confused entitlement about world domination succession planning, presented in the earnest register of a therapy session, is a good character joke. The therapist's reframing ('It feels like that to some of us sometimes') elevates it.

jokes.text: Listen to the words he used — 'Who's going to take over the world when I die?' It feels like that to some of us sometimes, doesn't it?
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has literally said he wants Scott to take over the world
jokes.punchline: The therapist normalizes 'take over the world' as a metaphor for parental pressure, completely missing (or deliberately ignoring) the literal meaning
jokes.explanation: The therapist's oblivious reframing of literal world domination as relatable parental pressure is a great deadpan beat. The earnestness of the professional context makes the collision funnier.

jokes.text: I don't know. I was thinking I like animals. Maybe I'd be a vet. / An evil vet? / No. Maybe work in a petting zoo. / An evil petting zoo? / You always do that!
jokes.setup: Scott expresses normal teenage career aspirations (veterinarian, petting zoo)
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil reflexively qualifies every option with 'evil' — it's an involuntary verbal tic; he literally cannot conceive of a non-evil version of anything. Scott's exasperation ('You always do that!') confirms it's a pattern.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The 'evil ___' running gag is introduced perfectly — it escalates (vet → petting zoo), and Scott's 'You always do that!' reveals this is a chronic pattern, deepening the character relationship. Dr. Evil's compulsion to evil-ify everything benign is pitch-perfect character comedy. High craft: the joke works through pure character logic.

jokes.text: I think he hates me. I really think he wants to kill me. / Scott, we don't want to kill each other in here. We might say that we do sometimes, but we really don't. / Actually, the boy's quite astute. I really am trying to kill him, but, so far, unsuccessfully. He's quite wily, like his old man.
jokes.setup: Scott voices the teenage fear that his parent wants to kill him; the therapist soothingly dismisses this as normal family hyperbole
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil confirms flatly that he genuinely is trying to kill Scott and has failed due to Scott's wiliness — treating filicide as a mild logistical challenge
jokes.explanation: Superb dark comedy. The therapist's well-meaning normalization ('we don't really mean it') is immediately torpedoed by Dr. Evil confirming the literal truth — and then paying Scott the backhanded compliment of being 'wily.' The escalation from therapy trope to actual homicidal confession, delivered with bureaucratic calm, is exactly what makes Dr. Evil work. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: The details of my life are quite inconsequential...
jokes.setup: Therapist and group ask Dr. Evil to share about his childhood
jokes.punchline: He refuses with grandiose pomposity before launching into an extremely consequential and bizarre monologue — the 'inconsequential' claim is instantly and spectacularly refuted
jokes.explanation: Perfect setup for the childhood monologue. The pompous dismissal ('quite inconsequential') before delivering the most consequential possible childhood makes the irony work immediately. The word 'inconsequential' doing so much ironic heavy lifting is elegant.
