jokes.text: My father was a relentlessly self-improving boulangerie owner from Belgium with low-grade narcolepsy and a penchant for buggery. My mother was a 15-year-old French prostitute named Chloe with webbed feet.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil begins his 'inconsequential' childhood backstory
jokes.punchline: The opening sentence alone piles on: Belgian baker, narcoleptic, buggery, teenage French prostitute mother, webbed feet — each detail more unexpected and specific than the last
jokes.explanation: The opening of the monologue is a masterwork of specificity-as-comedy. 'Boulangerie owner from Belgium' is funny on its own (why Belgian?), 'low-grade narcolepsy' adds precision to the absurdity, 'penchant for buggery' escalates into dark territory, and 'webbed feet' on the mother is the kind of non-sequitur detail that shows genuine comedy writing craft. Each element compounds the previous. Scores 8.0 on craft because it demonstrates how specificity, escalation, and deadpan delivery create comedy that's more than the sum of its parts.

jokes.text: My father would womanize, drink. He would make outrageous claims, like he invented the question mark. Sometimes he would accuse chestnuts of being lazy.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues describing his father's behavior
jokes.punchline: Among believable bad-father behavior (womanizing, drinking), he inserts 'invented the question mark' and 'accused chestnuts of being lazy' — the inanimate/absurd targets of the father's delusions are perfect
jokes.explanation: The 'chestnuts of being lazy' is one of the most purely funny lines in the film. The logic is perfect: a delusional man inventing the question mark is an absurd claim, but accusing chestnuts — specifically chestnuts — of laziness is a transcendent piece of absurdist writing. The specificity of 'chestnuts' (not trees, not nuts generally, chestnuts) is what makes it extraordinary. Borderline 8.5 craft.

jokes.text: My father would womanize, drink. He would make outrageous claims, like he invented the question mark. Sometimes he would accuse chestnuts of being lazy.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues describing his father's erratic behavior
jokes.punchline: The escalation from normal bad-dad behavior (womanizing, drinking) to absurdist specifics ('invented the question mark,' 'accused chestnuts of being lazy') is perfectly calibrated — each detail is more unhinged than the last
jokes.explanation: The apex of the Dr. Evil monologue. 'He would accuse chestnuts of being lazy' is one of the funniest lines Mike Myers ever wrote — it is utterly random yet internally consistent with the portrait of a delusional eccentric. 'He invented the question mark' is similarly perfect. The structure of mundane-to-absurd escalation within a list is flawless. This meets the 9+ standard: genuinely exceptional comedy writing, memorable, quotable, culturally referenced. 'Accuse chestnuts of being lazy' belongs in any discussion of great comedy lines.

jokes.text: ...the sort of general malaise that only the genius possess and the insane lament. My childhood was typical — summers in Rangoon, luge lessons. In the spring, we'd make meat helmets.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues the childhood monologue, pivoting from his father's pathologies to his own childhood activities
jokes.punchline: 'Summers in Rangoon, luge lessons' plays as exotic-but-plausible; 'we'd make meat helmets' is the left-turn absurd image that makes the whole list funny. The delivery of 'meat helmets' as mundane childhood craft is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: 'Meat helmets' is a quintessentially absurdist image delivered with total deadpan sincerity. The phrase is funny on its own, but positioned as a casual seasonal activity after 'Rangoon' and 'luge lessons' makes it land harder. The monologue's escalating absurdity continues to build masterfully.

jokes.text: When I was insolent, I was placed in a burlap bag and beaten with reeds. Pretty standard, really.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil describes his punishment as a child
jokes.punchline: 'Pretty standard, really' — the deadpan normalization of grotesque child abuse as routine
jokes.explanation: The economy of 'Pretty standard, really' as a tag for burlap bag beatings is excellent. Dr. Evil's breezy normalization of his own trauma is both funny and revealing — it explains everything about why he is the way he is, in one throwaway phrase.

jokes.text: At the age of 14, a Zoroastrian named Vilma ritualistically shaved my testicles. There really is nothing like a shorn scrotum. It's breathtaking. I suggest you try it.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil continues his childhood milestones
jokes.punchline: The Zoroastrian ritual scrotal shaving is absurd enough, but the pivot to genuine enthusiastic recommendation ('I suggest you try it') addressed directly to the therapy group makes it a complete joke — Dr. Evil is essentially endorsing scrotal shaving as a lifestyle product
jokes.explanation: 'There really is nothing like a shorn scrotum. It's breathtaking.' is one of the most quotable lines in the monologue. The specificity of 'Zoroastrian named Vilma' and the pivot to sincere recommendation ('I suggest you try it') addressed to strangers in group therapy is perfectly absurdist. High quotability.

jokes.text: You know, Miss Fagina. / I don't want to sound paranoid but I've had some bad relationships in the past...
jokes.setup: Vanessa is trying to have a serious conversation about jealousy and trust
jokes.punchline: She has to refer to the woman as 'Miss Fagina' with a straight face, the name itself being the recurring gag whenever it's said seriously
jokes.explanation: The name gag carries the comedic weight here rather than the writing itself. It's a running gag payoff — moderate.

jokes.text: I shagged her. / What? / I shagged her rotten, baby!
jokes.setup: Vanessa expresses jealousy about Alotta Fagina and asks Austin to reassure her
jokes.punchline: Austin instantly, cheerfully confesses and doubles down ('rotten') — his complete lack of social filter and inability to tell a comforting lie is entirely in character
jokes.explanation: Austin's confession functions as a character reveal — he literally cannot perform social deception. 'Shagged her rotten' as an enthusiastic elaboration rather than a backpedal is a good comedic choice. Solid character integration.

jokes.text: Saucer of milk, table two.
jokes.setup: Vanessa reacts indignantly to Austin's confession, saying she doesn't believe him ('She was repellent')
jokes.punchline: Austin calls out her cattiness with 'Saucer of milk, table two' — a British expression suggesting she's being bitchy/catty, delivered dry
jokes.explanation: A quick, dry British-idiom line. Works as a character beat — Austin calling out cattiness while himself being entirely oblivious to why she's upset. The irony gives it a little extra.

jokes.text: But did you use protection? / Of course. I had my nine-millimeter automatic. / I meant did you use a condom? / Only sailors use condoms, baby.
jokes.setup: Vanessa asks if Austin used protection — obviously meaning a condom
jokes.punchline: Austin takes 'protection' literally as a firearm reference; then when corrected, he dismisses condoms as a sailors-only artifact, revealing his 60s time-capsule attitude
jokes.explanation: Two-part joke with strong structure. The gun/condom misdirection is a classic double-meaning gag, but the capper 'Only sailors use condoms, baby' is what makes it excellent — it's not just ignorance, it's a specific, period-accurate misconception delivered with absolute conviction. Perfect character integration of the fish-out-of-water theme.

jokes.text: Not in the nineties. / Well, they should, those filthy beggars. They go from port to port.
jokes.setup: Vanessa corrects Austin that condoms aren't just for sailors
jokes.punchline: Austin doubles down, defending his sailor-condom theory with moralizing about sailors' promiscuity ('filthy beggars, go from port to port') — he doesn't update his worldview, he just argues for it more
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the gag — Austin's stubborn elaboration of his sailors theory is in character. 'Port to port' is a nice rhythmic flourish.

jokes.text: Check this guy out. Peace.
jokes.setup: Austin, in his conspicuously 60s outfit, apparently walks past someone in the 1990s
jokes.punchline: A modern person sees him and flashes a peace sign, treating him as an ironic retro figure — the visual anachronism of Austin's appearance in a contemporary setting gets a diegetic reaction
jokes.explanation: Light transitional gag — the film reminding us of Austin's visual anachronism. Slight, works as a beat between scenes.

jokes.text: Jimi Hendrix — deceased. Drugs. Janis Joplin. Deceased, alcohol. Mama Cass. Deceased, ham sandwich.
jokes.setup: Austin is apparently looking through a magazine or records, cataloging dead rock stars and their causes of death
jokes.punchline: The list follows a grim pattern (deceased + cause) until 'Mama Cass — deceased, ham sandwich.' The ham sandwich as cause of death (referencing the tabloid myth) delivered with the same clinical gravity as drugs and alcohol is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Classic list-joke structure where the third item subverts the pattern. The rhythm — 'Deceased, drugs. Deceased, alcohol. Deceased, ham sandwich.' — is impeccable, and 'ham sandwich' lands because of the pure bathetic deflation. The pattern and the break are executed with surgical economy.

jokes.text: Fall of the Berlin Wall, the first female British Prime Minister, end of apartheid. / Yeah, and I can't believe Liberace was gay. I mean, women loved him. I didn't see that one coming.
jokes.setup: Basil helpfully recaps major world events Austin missed while frozen
jokes.punchline: Austin's response focuses not on any of the earth-shattering events listed but on his shock at Liberace's homosexuality — a fact that was essentially universally obvious
jokes.explanation: Good fish-out-of-water character joke. Austin ignores the Berlin Wall and apartheid to process Liberace's sexuality — the wrong priority is the joke. 'I didn't see that one coming' applied to the most obviously gay entertainer in history is the right amount of absurd. Solid character integration.

jokes.text: Fall of the Berlin Wall, the first female British Prime Minister, end of apartheid. / Yeah, and I can't believe Liberace was gay. I mean, women loved him. I didn't see that one coming.
jokes.setup: Kensington lists major world events Austin missed during his 30-year freeze — implying he'll respond to the most significant ones
jokes.punchline: Austin's singular observation from the entire list is about Liberace's sexuality — missing all the geopolitical history to fixate on celebrity gossip, with the added irony that Liberace was famously flamboyant
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. The list of epochal events sets up an expectation that Austin will react to something meaningful. His total fixation on Liberace — and his genuine puzzlement ('women loved him') — is perfect character comedy. 'I didn't see that one coming' has an inadvertent double meaning (not seeing homosexuality coming / not seeing the joke coming). One of the reel's strong standout moments. At the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Do you think she's prettier than me? / Who? / You know who. / Oh, the Italian bird. / No, baby. She's rancid. I think you're shagadelic, baby. You're switched on. You're smashing.
jokes.setup: Vanessa fishes for reassurance about Alotta Fagina while they're apparently in a tour group at Virtucon
jokes.punchline: Austin's attempt at reassurance devolves into a pile-on against Alotta ('rancid') and then calling Vanessa 'shagadelic' — his compliments are indistinguishable from his insults in register
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Austin's vocabulary of praise ('shagadelic,' 'switched on,' 'smashing') is itself the joke, the 60s slang deployed as sincere compliment. Light.

jokes.text: She's the village bicycle. Everyone's had a ride.
jokes.setup: Austin is still trying to reassure Vanessa about Alotta Fagina mid-Virtucon tour
jokes.punchline: He reassures her by calling Alotta 'the village bicycle' — which is both an insult to Alotta and an accidental admission that Austin himself has 'had a ride,' undermining the reassurance entirely
jokes.explanation: The 'village bicycle' idiom is the right level of crude-British for the film, and the self-incriminating logic (Austin is included in 'everyone') adds an ironic layer. Good economy.

jokes.text: Does that make you horny? / Not now, Austin.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is demonstrating the Vulcan drill — a massive phallic subterranean drilling device
jokes.punchline: Austin's immediate sexualization of an enormous drill is perfectly timed, and Vanessa's weary 'Not now, Austin' acknowledges both the innuendo and the timing
jokes.explanation: Classic Austin innuendo gag — his inability to suppress sexual commentary regardless of context is a core character trait. 'Not now, Austin' as the exasperated straight-man response is well-placed and implies this happens all the time. The visual of the phallic drill sells it.

jokes.text: Check it out, butt-head. This chick has three boobs.
jokes.setup: Scott and presumably his friend are in Dr. Evil's lair watching something (likely a fembot or henchwoman)
jokes.punchline: Scott's reaction to the exotic supervillain lair is the completely mundane teenage boy response — fixating on extra breasts, addressed to his friend as 'butt-head'
jokes.explanation: Scott's perpetual teenage normalcy as a contrast to his supervillain surroundings is his comedy engine. The three-boob observation (referencing Total Recall) is a juvenile joke that's exactly right for Scott's character.

jokes.text: How many butts does she have?
jokes.setup: Scott tells his friend the woman has three boobs
jokes.punchline: His friend's response is to wonder about proportional number of butts — following the same logic (extra body parts) but to the wrong conclusion
jokes.explanation: Quick, dumb-funny tag. The logic of 'if three boobs then how many butts?' is the right level of teenage stupidity. Good economy — it's a one-liner that earns its laugh.

jokes.text: Scott tells his dad about his day: Sweet Jay got in a fight because they 'don't speak French' — the whole confrontation described in teenager-speak ('he's all,' 'I'm like,' 'they're all,' 'we're like,' 'Make me,' 'It was cool.')
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil asks Scott how his day was, as a father might
jokes.punchline: Scott's story is delivered entirely in 90s teenager cadence, full of non-drama drama ('he's all,' 'I'm like'), and Dr. Evil responds: 'Fascinating.' — the supervillain treating a teenager's mundane arcade fight with the same gravity he applies to world domination
jokes.explanation: Dr. Evil's 'Fascinating' in response to a teenager's pointless story is a great character beat — his grandiose deadpan applied to the trivial. The 90s slang dialect is well-observed and Scott's obliviousness to the irony of narrating a nothing story to a supervillain is good writing.

jokes.text: My friend Sweet Jay took me to that video arcade in town. They don't speak English, so Jay got into a fight... [Scott's rambling anecdote]
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil asks Scott about his day, expecting something sinister
jokes.punchline: Scott's response is a completely banal, rambling teenage anecdote about an arcade fight — the mundanity is the entire joke, landing against the backdrop of world domination planning
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Scott — the absolute normality of his teenage experience against the backdrop of an underground volcano lair is funny. The joke runs slightly long, which hurts economy, but the character contrast is well-executed.

jokes.text: What are your plans for this evening? / I thought I'd stay in. There's a good titty movie on Skinimax.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil asks Scott about his evening plans, apparently expecting evil schemes
jokes.punchline: Scott's plan is to watch softcore cable porn. Dr. Evil's aspirations for his son clash with Scott's total contentment with the absolute minimum.
jokes.explanation: 'Skinimax' (Cinemax's nickname) is a period-accurate detail. The contrast between evil empire and teenage cable TV routine is the joke. Functional.

jokes.text: Are you feeding him? Why don't you just kill him? / I have an even better idea. I'm going to place him in an easily escapable situation involving an overly elaborate and exotic death.
jokes.setup: Scott sees Austin Powers captured and makes the logical suggestion: just kill him
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil announces his plan is to put Austin in an 'easily escapable situation involving an overly elaborate and exotic death' — literally describing the Bond villain trope by name, acknowledging its stupidity while committing to it anyway
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the film and one of the best in this reel. The genius is Dr. Evil explicitly naming the trope he's about to commit — 'easily escapable situation involving an overly elaborate and exotic death' — as if it's a reasonable plan. This is the film's core meta-commentary on spy movies crystallized perfectly. The specificity of 'overly elaborate and exotic' shows real writing craft — these are exactly the right words. Scott's pragmatic pushback makes it even better. This comfortably earns its 8+ score: it's the film's thesis statement as comedy, delivered through perfect character logic.

jokes.text: Why don't you just shoot him now? I'll go get a gun. We'll shoot him together. It'll be fun. Bang! Dead. Done. / One more peep out of you and you are grounded, mister, and I am not joking.
jokes.setup: Scott presses his case for simply shooting Austin rather than the elaborate plan
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil threatens to ground Scott with full parental authority — a supervillain doing regular dad discipline is absurd; 'I am not joking' as a sincere parental threat from a man who just described an elaborate death trap is perfect
jokes.explanation: Brilliant juxtaposition — 'you are grounded, mister' from a supervillain in his underground lair. The domestic parenting tone dropped into the Bond-villain setting is perfect character comedy. 'I am not joking' as a sincere parental threat is exceptionally funny in context. High craft: could only be this character in this situation.

jokes.text: Release the sharks! You'll notice that all the sharks have laser beams attached to their heads. I figure every creature deserves a warm meal.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has captured Austin and announces his execution method: sharks with laser beams
jokes.punchline: The 'warm meal' justification for arming sharks with lasers — Dr. Evil frames equipping sharks for murder as animal welfare
jokes.explanation: Dr. Evil's animal-welfare rationale for laser-armed sharks is a lovely character moment — his logic is internally consistent and completely insane. The 'warm meal' phrase is a good punchline. Sharks with laser beams is a cultural touchstone of this film.

jokes.text: When you were frozen, they were put on the endangered species list. We tried to get some, but it would've taken months to clear up the red tape.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil requests sharks with laser beams; a henchman explains the problem
jokes.punchline: The bureaucratic obstacle to obtaining murder sharks is government red tape due to the Endangered Species Act — the mundane regulatory compliance problem facing a supervillain
jokes.explanation: The joke is that environmental protection laws apply equally to supervillain procurement. 'Months to clear up the red tape' for murder sharks is a good bureaucracy-meets-evil gag.

jokes.text: I have one simple request, and that is to have sharks with frickin' laser beams attached to their heads!
jokes.setup: Henchman explains they couldn't get sharks due to red tape
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil explodes with the specific outrage that his 'one simple request' — sharks with laser beams — was denied. The word 'frickin'' (a child-safe profanity) in the middle of a megalomaniacal rant is the specific comedic touch.
jokes.explanation: The most quotable line in the film. 'Frickin'' as the chosen almost-profanity of an actual evil supervillain is a perfect character choice — slightly softened, oddly domestic, completely unexpected. 'One simple request' applied to laser-shark procurement is the right level of absurd grandiosity. This is a cultural touchstone line. The impact score is a 9 (not 10) because it works better as a standalone quote than as a room-erupting moment in context — the buildup is good but the scene carries the gag over several beats.

jokes.text: Evidently, my cycloptic colleague informs me that that can't be done. Can you remind me what I pay you people for? Honestly, throw me a bone here. What do we have?
jokes.setup: After the laser-shark tirade, Dr. Evil is told it can't be done
jokes.punchline: His pivot to exasperated middle-management frustration ('throw me a bone here') after a megalomaniacal rage is a perfect tonal collapse — 'cycloptic colleague' is an oddly formal descriptor that also gets a laugh
jokes.explanation: 'Throw me a bone here' from a supervillain is a good management-speak deflation gag. 'Cycloptic colleague' as a formal but accurate descriptor of a one-eyed henchman is a nice word-choice laugh.

jokes.text: Sea bass. / ... / They are mutated sea bass. / Really? Are they ill-tempered? / Absolutely. / That's a start.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil asks what they have instead of sharks; the answer is sea bass
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil's acceptance of mutated sea bass contingent on their being 'ill-tempered' — not on their lethality, their size, or their mutations, but their disposition — is a perfect comedic escalation, and 'That's a start' as grudging acceptance is the right understated close
jokes.explanation: Possibly the best-structured joke in this reel. The beat of 'Sea bass' (pause) 'They are mutated sea bass' — with the pause before 'mutated' doing comedic work — followed by Dr. Evil's specific inquiry about temperament ('Are they ill-tempered?') as the deciding factor is brilliantly written. 'Absolutely.' / 'That's a start.' is a perfect deadpan close. The joke works because Dr. Evil has very specific requirements for his murder animals, and 'ill-tempered' is both logical within his worldview and completely absurd. Earns its 8+ craft score: the structure alone is excellent, and the character integration is perfect.

jokes.text: All right, guard, begin the unnecessarily slow-moving dipping mechanism.
jokes.setup: Austin and Vanessa are captured and are being lowered toward the sea bass tank
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil literally names his own device 'the unnecessarily slow-moving dipping mechanism' — acknowledging the cliché while ordering it deployed
jokes.explanation: One of the film's sharpest meta-jokes. 'Unnecessarily slow-moving dipping mechanism' is comedy gold precisely because it's self-aware — the name acknowledges the purpose (slow = escapable) while ordering it anyway. Like the 'easily escapable situation' joke, Dr. Evil understands the cliché and commits to it, which is funnier than if he were oblivious. Earns 8+ on craft: the specific naming ('unnecessarily') shows real writing precision.

jokes.text: Close the tank! / Aren't you even going to watch them? They could get away. / I'm going to leave them alone and not actually witness them dying. I'm just going to assume it all went to plan.
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil orders Austin left in the dipping mechanism and turns to leave
jokes.punchline: Scott points out the obvious Bond-villain mistake; Dr. Evil openly acknowledges he's going to make it anyway, stating his plan to 'assume it all went to plan' as if this were sound operational doctrine
jokes.explanation: This is the culmination of the Scott/Dr. Evil kill-him-now thread. Scott is right, Dr. Evil knows he's right, and Dr. Evil is going to do the wrong thing anyway — not out of stupidity but out of a commitment to genre conventions he will not relinquish. 'I'm just going to assume it all went to plan' is a devastating line because it's both a Bond villain parody AND a universal human tendency to avoid witnessing the consequences of one's decisions.

jokes.text: Close the tank! Aren't you even going to watch them? They could get away. / I'm going to leave them alone and not actually witness them dying. I'm just going to assume it all went to plan.
jokes.setup: Scott protests as Dr. Evil turns to leave without watching Austin die
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil explicitly states his intention to not watch and to 'assume it all went to plan' — directly naming and committing to another Bond villain cliché (leaving before confirming the kill)
jokes.explanation: Dr. Evil's sustained commitment to Bond-villain tropes while Scott provides the voice of reason is a running meta-gag that keeps building. 'I'm just going to assume it all went to plan' is a perfect deadpan encapsulation of villain stupidity. Each of Scott's objections sharpens the joke.

jokes.text: I have a gun in my room. You give me five seconds, I'll get it. I'll come back, boom! I'll blow their brains out. / You just don't get it, do you?
jokes.setup: Scott makes one more plea to just shoot Austin, now with a specific actionable plan
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil dismisses Scott's entirely reasonable execution plan with 'You just don't get it, do you?' — the same phrase someone would use to dismiss a philistine, applied to the person who wants to actually commit murder efficiently
jokes.explanation: 'You just don't get it, do you?' as the dismissal of Scott's pragmatic murder plan is excellent — it inverts the cliché (Scott is the one who 'gets it'; Dr. Evil is the one who doesn't). The callback to Vanessa saying the same thing to Austin earlier in the reel adds an extra layer.

jokes.text: Knock knock. / Who's there? / Let me tell you a little story about a man named 'shh.' Even before you start, that was a preemptive 'shh.' Just know I have a whole bag of 'shh' with your name on it.
jokes.setup: Austin and Vanessa are trapped in the dipping mechanism above the sea bass tank; Austin initiates a knock-knock joke to lighten the mood
jokes.punchline: The knock-knock joke is a feint — the actual joke is Austin's escalating command for silence ('shh') preemptively deployed before Vanessa can speak
jokes.explanation: The 'whole bag of shh with your name on it' is a good line — the escalation from one 'shh' to a 'whole bag' of them, plus 'preemptive shh,' is well-structured. The knock-knock setup misdirects nicely.

jokes.text: What's your plan? / First, I plan to soil myself, then I'm going to regroup and come up with a new plan.
jokes.setup: Vanessa asks Austin, the spy hero, what his plan is to escape the dipping mechanism
jokes.punchline: His plan begins with soiling himself — not as a ruse, apparently genuinely — before regrouping. The phased approach (soil, regroup, plan) delivered with spy-seriousness is the gag.
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the spy competence expectation. The structure ('First... then...') mimics a tactical briefing, making the 'soil myself' beat land harder. Austin's earnest phase-one of soiling himself is funnier than outright cowardice because of its clinical delivery.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. I always have this with me, just in case. / I get it. I have bad teeth. / No, Austin. The floss is to swing ourselves onto the ledge.
jokes.setup: Vanessa produces the dental kit from earlier; Austin immediately misreads its use as a dental judgment
jokes.punchline: Austin takes the floss as a comment on his teeth rather than an escape tool — a callback to both the dentistry gear scene and Austin's notorious British dental reputation
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback to two earlier jokes simultaneously — the dental gadget briefing scene and the implicit bad-teeth gag. Austin's self-conscious 'I get it, I have bad teeth' shows character vulnerability while delivering a callback payoff. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. I always have this with me, just in case. I get it. I have bad teeth. / No, Austin. The floss is to swing ourselves onto the ledge.
jokes.setup: Austin produces the dental floss from earlier; he immediately misunderstands and thinks it's being referenced as commentary on his teeth
jokes.punchline: His defensive 'I get it. I have bad teeth.' — a callback to the earlier dentistry gag — shows his greatest insecurity is not being lowered into a tank of mutant sea bass, but his dental hygiene
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff. The earlier dentistry gag pays off here with Austin's self-conscious reaction: in a life-or-death moment, his primary concern is that the floss comment might be about his teeth. This reveals more character (his vanity/insecurity) while delivering a laugh. Well-constructed.

jokes.text: Not a good time to lose one's head. / Indeed. / That's not the way to get ahead in life. / It's a shame he wasn't more headstrong. / He'll never be the head of a major corporation. / That'll do.
jokes.setup: A guard has apparently been decapitated during the escape
jokes.punchline: Austin launches into an escalating series of decapitation puns ('lose one's head,' 'get ahead,' 'headstrong,' 'head of a major corporation'), each landing in rapid succession until Vanessa calls it with 'That'll do'
jokes.explanation: Classic escalating pun sequence — four 'head' puns deployed in quick succession before the killjoy 'That'll do' cuts it off. The structure is the joke: Austin's compulsion to run a pun into the ground, and Vanessa's exasperation as the straight man. Well-timed if not especially original.

jokes.text: Whatever happens, I want you to know that I feel really bad about that Italian bird. What I'm trying to say is that if you want me to be a one-woman man, that's just groovy, baby. Behave.
jokes.setup: In what may be their last moment before death, Austin chooses to revisit the Alotta Fagina affair
jokes.punchline: His attempted sincere romantic declaration is entirely in his own idiolect — 'groovy, baby' and 'behave' — and the fact that facing death he's most concerned about being understood about the Italian shag is perfectly Austin
jokes.explanation: A closing character beat — Austin's romantic sincerity expressed entirely through his own anachronistic vocabulary. 'That's just groovy, baby' as a commitment to monogamy is perfectly Austin. Moderate craft; functions as emotional-comedic beat.

jokes.text: Scott says 'Blow me' — then quickly corrects himself to 'Show me'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil asks Scott if he wants to see what Daddy does for a living — a sincere parental moment
jokes.punchline: Scott appears to say 'Blow me' (a crude dismissal/sexual innuendo) before correcting to 'Show me', leaving the double entendre hanging
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — two words do all the work. The misdirection is sharp: the audience registers the obscenity before the correction, and the comedic beat is the gap between what we heard and what was 'meant'. Scott's sulky teenager persona makes it fit perfectly — it sounds exactly like something he'd say. High rewatch value because on second viewing you anticipate it.

jokes.text: Fembot seductively asks Austin if he wants to have a little fun; Austin responds 'No, actually... I have to save the world.'
jokes.setup: Fembots are irresistibly seductive; Austin has been established as a man who cannot resist women
jokes.punchline: Austin calmly declines — prioritizing world-saving over sex — a complete reversal of his established character, delivered with total nonchalance
jokes.explanation: Works because the entire film has established Austin as incapable of resisting women — so casually brushing off a fembot to save the world is a character-based reversal. The understatement ('No, actually... I have to save the world') is pitch-perfect. High character integration score because only Austin's specific characterization makes this land.

jokes.text: Austin, surrounded by seductive fembots, mutters 'Is it cold in here?' — clearly fighting arousal by focusing on a mundane question
jokes.setup: Austin is surrounded by irresistible fembots and is visibly struggling not to succumb to them
jokes.punchline: He attempts to distract himself with the most mundane possible question — implying he is using the cold-shower mental technique against his libido
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat. The mundane question as a coping mechanism is funny in context, though it's a mild laugh rather than a big one. Works as part of the escalating fembot resistance sequence.

jokes.text: Austin, still resisting fembots, mutters 'Baseball, cold showers.'
jokes.setup: Austin is using classic male distraction techniques to suppress his arousal around the fembots
jokes.punchline: He lists the clichéd mental tricks men supposedly use — 'baseball, cold showers' — as if reading from a manual of unsexy thoughts
jokes.explanation: Part of the escalating fembot resistance sequence. The joke is the clichéd nature of the distraction — it's observational comedy about male psychology dressed as character comedy. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: A guard tells Austin to give up; Austin responds 'Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day.'
jokes.setup: Austin is being told to surrender while mentally fighting his arousal from the fembots
jokes.punchline: He invokes the maximally unarousing mental image of Margaret Thatcher naked — the most anti-erotic image an Englishman of Austin's era could conjure — delivered mid-action as if it's a tactical maneuver
jokes.explanation: One of the film's best jokes. The specificity is everything — 'Margaret Thatcher naked on a cold day' is the perfect maximally-unarousing image for a British swinger of Austin's generation, and delivering it as a battle cry mid-action is inspired. It's completely character-specific (only Austin, only British, only this era), economical (seven words), and utterly original. Easily quotable and has become a genuine cultural touchstone from the film. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality — arguably exceeds it.

jokes.text: Austin tells the fembots 'Au contraire, baby. I think you can't resist me' — reversing their seduction logic
jokes.setup: The fembots are pleading for Austin to stay and not resist them
jokes.punchline: Austin flips the seduction dynamic, claiming it's actually THEY who can't resist HIM — his confidence is so total he reframes being surrounded by killer sex robots as a situation where he's the one in control
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Austin's delusional confidence is his defining trait and this is a good expression of it. The reversal logic is clean. Not as sharp as the Thatcher line but a good button on the fembot sequence.

jokes.text: Austin's rambling explanation to Vanessa about the fembots: 'smoke started to come out of their jumblies... cross-mojonations... their heads started exploding... I ended up in my knickers'
jokes.setup: Vanessa has found Austin in a compromising situation; he needs to explain what happened
jokes.punchline: His explanation uses made-up words ('jumblies', 'cross-mojonations'), Austin-isms that make the absurd fembot plot sound even more ridiculous, and ends with him in his underwear — the explanation is simultaneously accurate and utterly unbelievable in its phrasing
jokes.explanation: Mike Myers' invented vocabulary is a consistent comic engine. 'Jumblies' and 'cross-mojonations' are genuinely funny Austin-specific words. The structure — a rambling excuse that's actually true — works well. Slightly bloated (could be tighter) but delivers laughs throughout.

jokes.text: Vanessa says 'I believe you' with complete sincerity after Austin's insane fembot explanation
jokes.setup: Austin has delivered an utterly unbelievable, jargon-filled explanation involving fembots, 'mojonations', and exploding heads
jokes.punchline: Vanessa immediately and calmly says 'I believe you' — she has apparently been in Austin's world long enough that this is entirely plausible to her
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man economy. Three words do maximum work by inverting the expected skepticism. Vanessa's deadpan acceptance is funnier than any argument could be. Good structure: the longer Austin's explanation, the funnier the flat acceptance becomes.

jokes.text: Mission control announces 'Begin initial surface penetration' — clearly double-entendre language for the drill probe
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil's volcanic drill (Project Vulcan) is being deployed as a doomsday weapon
jokes.punchline: The technical language for drilling — 'initial surface penetration' — is delivered as if clinical but reads as sexual innuendo
jokes.explanation: Classic Austin Powers innuendo gag — the film frequently uses spy/military technical language as sexual double entendre. Functional but among the more routine deployments of this running joke. Low character integration since any technician could say it.

jokes.text: Guard, while running from gunfire, shouts 'Oh, I tripped!' — a weirdly polite self-narration during a deadly firefight
jokes.setup: An intense action sequence with guards running and shooting
jokes.punchline: One guard stops to announce 'Oh, I tripped!' as if reporting a minor mishap to no one in particular — a comically mundane observation in a life-or-death situation
jokes.explanation: A quick, absurdist beat that works by injecting a mundane social convention ('I tripped!') into an action sequence. It's the kind of understated British-ism that fits the film's sensibility. Quick laugh, doesn't overstay its welcome.

jokes.text: Austin shouts 'Judo!' before performing a judo chop — announcing his move like a video game character
jokes.setup: Austin needs to destroy the probe in a tense action moment
jokes.punchline: He announces 'Judo!' as a battle cry before attacking — as if naming the martial art makes the move more official
jokes.explanation: Funny in its absurd brevity — one word, maximum commitment. The judo chop is an Austin Powers signature move (callbacks to earlier reels), so announcing it formally elevates the gag. The rewatch bonus is because the anticipation of seeing it happen after the announcement adds to it.

jokes.text: While hunting Dr. Evil, Austin sings the Meow Mix jingle: 'I want chicken, I want liver, Meow Mix, Meow Mix, please deliver'
jokes.setup: Austin is on a deadly serious mission to capture Dr. Evil in a tense self-destructing complex
jokes.punchline: He casually sings the Meow Mix cat food commercial jingle while stalking his nemesis — a completely incongruous moment of whimsy in the climax
jokes.explanation: Excellent tonal whiplash — the Meow Mix jingle is maximally undignified and childish for a climactic spy confrontation. It works because it's entirely consistent with Austin's chaotic, childlike character while being completely at odds with the tension of the scene. The specific choice of Meow Mix (not just any song) is inspired — it's catchy, recognizable, and deeply silly.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil's speech: 'We're not so different, you and I' — playing the classic villain monologue completely straight
jokes.setup: Austin has cornered Dr. Evil; this is the climactic confrontation
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil launches into the archetypal villain speech ('We're not so different, you and I') — a cliché so familiar the film weaponizes it as self-aware parody of spy film conventions
jokes.explanation: The humor comes from recognizing the trope. Dr. Evil is a parody villain and leaning into the villain speech archetype is on-brand. Functional meta-comedy but not especially inspired — the film does sharper meta work elsewhere.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil argues that free love and swinging parties are now considered 'evil' in the nineties — using Austin's own values against him
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is making a philosophical argument to destabilize Austin
jokes.punchline: The irony that the genuinely 'evil' character is correctly pointing out that Austin's innocent 60s hedonism is now socially condemned — making Austin's values sound worse than Dr. Evil's world domination scheme in cultural terms
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever satirical writing — the argument has actual logic and the irony is real. Austin's rebuttal ('freedom and responsibility... it's a very groovy time') is both heartfelt and absurd. This is smarter comedy than the film usually attempts, though it's more wit than big laughs.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil: 'There's nothing more pathetic than an aging hipster.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is responding to Austin's sincere defense of 60s freedom and responsibility
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil — a bald, scar-faced, spandex-wearing megalomaniac who lives in a volcano — delivers a withering observation about aging hipsters with complete moral authority
jokes.explanation: The irony is delicious — Dr. Evil calling anyone pathetic while wearing a Nehru jacket and demanding world domination. The line itself is sharp and quotable, and it works on two levels: as a genuine observation and as an absurd non-sequitur from this particular speaker. Good economy (nine words) and high character integration — only Dr. Evil's specific absurdity makes this funny.

jokes.text: Austin responds to Dr. Evil's taunt with 'All right, baldy. Shut your cakehole.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has delivered a cutting philosophical observation about Austin
jokes.punchline: Austin's rebuttal completely abandons the philosophical debate — 'baldy. Shut your cakehole' is the least intellectual possible response to a treatise on the failure of freedom
jokes.explanation: Perfect character response — when outargued, Austin just resorts to British playground insults. 'Cakehole' is a brilliantly specific British-ism that fits Austin perfectly. The bathos of going from 'freedom failed' to 'shut your cakehole' is funny and very character-true.

jokes.text: Scott asks if he can take his Sega — in the middle of a hostage standoff between Austin and Dr. Evil
jokes.setup: Austin is being held at gunpoint by Dr. Evil; Vanessa declares Austin should go ahead without worrying about her
jokes.punchline: Scott, being used as a hostage himself, asks 'I can take my Sega, right, Dad?' — his biggest concern in a life-or-death situation is his video game console
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Scott Evil is the film's sharpest running joke — a sulky, profoundly normal teenager trapped in a supervillain's lair. The Sega question perfectly captures his oblivious teenage priorities mid-crisis. It's simultaneously a character joke about Scott AND a parody of hostage drama conventions. High character integration — only Scott's established personality makes this work.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil: 'Not really. Kill the little bastard. See what I care.'
jokes.setup: Austin says 'it seems the tables have turned again, Dr. Evil' — using Scott as leverage
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil instantly and cheerfully orders Scott killed — revealing he genuinely does not care about his son at all despite the earlier 'bonding' attempts
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny in equal measure. The cheerful indifference ('See what I care') is more damning than active cruelty. Dr. Evil's character is defined by his inability to perform normal human emotions convincingly, and this is a crisp expression of that. The 'tables have turned' callback being immediately deflated is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Scott: 'But, Dad, we just had a breakthrough in group.' Dr. Evil: 'I had the group liquidated, you little shit. They were insolent.'
jokes.setup: Scott protests Dr. Evil's order to kill him by citing their recent therapy progress
jokes.punchline: Dr. Evil reveals he had the entire therapy group killed for being 'insolent' — the mundane word 'insolent' applied to mass murder of a therapy group is perfect dark comedy
jokes.explanation: Among the film's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Scott's reasonable protest (therapy progress!) is answered with revelation that the therapeutic resource has been eliminated, using the pettiest possible justification ('They were insolent'). The gap between 'we had a breakthrough in group' and 'I had the group liquidated' is a masterclass in dark comedy escalation. 'You little shit' is also Dr. Evil at his most honest. High character integration — only Dr. Evil could simultaneously reference therapy and mass murder this casually.

jokes.text: Scott: 'I hate you! I wish I was never artificially created in a lab.' Dr. Evil: 'Scott, that hurts Daddy when you say that, honestly.'
jokes.setup: Typical teenage tantrum exchange between son and parent — 'I hate you! I wish I was never born!'
jokes.punchline: Scott substitutes 'born' with 'artificially created in a lab' — the specific, clinical detail transforms a cliché teen line into something uniquely surreal. Dr. Evil's wounded response ('that hurts Daddy, honestly') plays this earnestly.
jokes.explanation: One of the film's finest jokes. It takes the universal 'I wish I was never born' teenage cliché and makes it specific to the unique circumstances of this family — the clinical replacement word ('artificially created in a lab') is both absurd and entirely logical given who Dr. Evil is. Dr. Evil's sincere hurt in response ('Scott, that hurts Daddy when you say that, honestly') is perfect deadpan. The 'honestly' tacked on at the end is a beautiful touch — it implies Dr. Evil knows Scott doesn't believe he has real feelings. Genuinely quotable and character-essential.

jokes.text: Number Two confronts Dr. Evil: 'I've spent 30 years turning this two-bit evil empire into a world-class multinational. I was going to have a cover story in Forbes.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has just destroyed his own plan; Number Two is furious
jokes.punchline: Number Two's grievance is not about the evil — it's about the missed Forbes cover story. His legitimate business ambitions for an evil organization are played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Very funny concept — the evil organization's COO is upset not about world domination failure but about missing a magazine profile. The Forbes detail is perfect and specific. Number Two as the frustrated middle manager of evil is a great character note consistently played throughout the film.

jokes.text: Number Two: 'You don't realize there is no world anymore. It's only corporations.'
jokes.setup: Number Two is arguing that Dr. Evil's world domination plan is obsolete
jokes.punchline: His point — that corporations have already achieved what Dr. Evil is attempting through legitimate business — is both a satirical observation about capitalism AND a funny inversion where the villain's plan is derided as naively idealistic
jokes.explanation: Smart satirical comedy — the idea that world domination is quaint compared to corporate hegemony is genuinely sharp. Gets a knowing laugh from an audience that understands the joke about capitalism. Slightly more wit than raw comedy.

jokes.text: Austin delivers a 'Judo chop!' to Number Two — again announcing the move
jokes.setup: Number Two threatens Austin after his speech
jokes.punchline: Austin shouts 'Judo chop!' — the running gag of announcing his signature move before executing it
jokes.explanation: Running gag that earns its repeat. The judo chop announcement is pure Austin Powers — the second instance in this reel reinforces it as a character signature. Diminishing returns slightly versus the first instance, but still delivers because of timing and commitment.

jokes.text: Post-escape romantic moment: 'I love you, Mr. Powers.' / 'And I love you, Mrs. Powers.'
jokes.setup: They've just escaped a self-destructing complex — tense action sequence
jokes.punchline: The immediate pivot to tender domestic address ('Mrs. Powers') implies they've gotten married in the chaos — played as a completely natural conclusion to the adventure
jokes.explanation: Sweet more than funny, but the abruptness of the marriage reveal gets a mild laugh. Functions more as a plot beat than a comedy beat, but the compressed timeline (we didn't see the wedding) earns a chuckle.

jokes.text: Basil calls during the honeymoon; Austin says 'No, not at all, Basil. Did you get that fruit basket I sent you?' followed by an extended back-and-forth about a fruit basket and 'nice rack'
jokes.setup: Basil has interrupted Austin's honeymoon with urgent spy business
jokes.punchline: Austin derails the urgent spy briefing with domestic trivialities — did Basil get the fruit basket? Should he send some to his mum? — before the innuendo payoff: 'Yes, Basil, nice rack' (referring to a wine rack, presumably, while sounding like a physical compliment)
jokes.explanation: Good running business — Austin's social niceties completely overwhelming spy protocol. The fruit basket escalating to 'send some to my mother' is good character comedy. 'Nice rack' is a mild double entendre payoff. Entertaining but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Basil says they sent too much in the fruit basket; Vanessa says 'I'm gonna have to send some to my mother'
jokes.setup: Mission debrief is happening; there's urgent news about Dr. Evil escaping
jokes.punchline: The spy conversation has become a discussion about redistributing excess fruit basket contents — completely mundane logistics discussed as if they're important
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing extension of the fruit basket gag but doesn't add much beyond the initial joke. The humor is in the mundane but it's stretched slightly thin here.

jokes.text: Austin and Vanessa receive a 'bizarre drawing' as a gift — the audience presumably sees it; characters are baffled
jokes.setup: Basil has delivered multiple gifts; the last one is a mysterious drawing
jokes.punchline: The drawing is apparently so bizarre and inexplicable that neither Austin nor Vanessa can identify what it is or who sent it — visual gag dependent on audience seeing the image
jokes.explanation: Difficult to fully assess from transcript alone — this is a visual gag that depends on what the drawing actually shows. As presented in transcript, it reads as a mild absurdist beat. Likely lands better on screen than it reads here.

jokes.text: Basil tells Austin he's to be knighted by the Queen; Austin responds 'Very shagadelic!'
jokes.setup: Basil formally delivers the news of a royal knighthood — a solemn, prestigious honor
jokes.punchline: Austin's response to being knighted is the same word he uses for everything good — 'shagadelic' — reducing a royal honor to the same level as a good cup of tea
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy. 'Shagadelic' is Austin's signature word and applying it to royal honors is appropriately absurd. Not the film's freshest use of the word by this point, but it still works as character consistency.

jokes.text: Austin asks if Vanessa felt the same way when she first saw him. She says: 'Actually, I couldn't stop staring at your teeth.'
jokes.setup: Austin asks a romantic question — did she feel the same magnetic attraction he felt for her?
jokes.punchline: Vanessa's answer is not romantic longing but visceral horror at Austin's infamously terrible teeth — a physical defect that's been a running visual gag throughout the film
jokes.explanation: Good callback joke. The setup is a sincere romantic question that Austin delivers earnestly, making the deflation funnier. 'Couldn't stop staring at your teeth' is delivered deadpan and works as both a visual callback and character moment — Vanessa is becoming more comfortable being honest with Austin.

jokes.text: Dr. Evil throws a shoe at Austin; Austin, injured, says 'Who throws a shoe? Honestly.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil attacks Austin — presumably with a weapon or something threatening
jokes.punchline: The weapon is a shoe. Austin's response — 'Who throws a shoe? Honestly.' — is a baffled, almost offended reaction to the indignity and absurdity of being attacked with footwear
jokes.explanation: Genuinely exceptional — one of the film's most quotable lines and a genuine comedy gem. The genius is the offended confusion: Austin has just escaped a self-destructing supervillain complex, fought killer fembots, and defeated henchmen — but being hit with a shoe is the thing that baffles him morally. 'Honestly' at the end is perfect indignant understatement. High originality because the shoe throw is a completely unexpected choice, and the specific indignation of the response elevates it beyond a simple physical gag.

jokes.text: Austin responds to Dr. Evil: 'You fight like a woman.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil has just attacked Austin with a shoe
jokes.punchline: Austin's taunt — 'You fight like a woman' — is itself ironic given the context: being hit by a shoe is not exactly masculine combat, but Austin's criticism of the technique is characteristically oblivious to his own circumstances
jokes.explanation: Decent follow-on from the shoe joke, but significantly weaker than 'Who throws a shoe?'. The line is a mild laugh and somewhat dated in its humor. Works in context but isn't memorable.

jokes.text: Austin and Vanessa look at stars; Austin says 'Yeah, and that looks just like Uranus.'
jokes.setup: Vanessa romantically identifies a constellation; Austin plays along
jokes.punchline: 'Uranus' — the planet name as a pun on 'your anus' — is delivered by Austin with his characteristic enthusiasm, treating it as an innocent astronomical observation
jokes.explanation: The Uranus/your anus pun is the oldest joke in astronomy — it requires essentially zero craft to deploy. The film earns slight credit for Austin's earnest delivery making it fit his character, but the base joke has been in every schoolboy's arsenal since forever. Among the weakest jokes in this reel.

jokes.text: Cut to Dr. Evil in his rocket: 'I'm gonna get you, Austin Powers. It's frickin' freezing in here, Mr. Bigglesworth.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil is making his dramatic villain escape/vow of revenge
jokes.punchline: His menacing monologue is immediately deflated by a mundane complaint about the temperature, delivered to his cat — 'frickin' freezing' undermines the entire dramatic moment
jokes.explanation: Excellent bathos. The villain revenge monologue is a sacred spy film tradition — puncturing it with 'it's frickin' freezing in here, Mr. Bigglesworth' is inspired. The specific detail of Dr. Evil complaining about temperature to his hairless cat rather than to any human is perfectly absurd. 'Mr. Bigglesworth' as the cat's name adds another layer of comedy. This line is highly quotable and captures exactly why Dr. Evil works as a character — genuinely menacing one moment, comically mundane the next.

jokes.text: Extended photo shoot sequence — Austin directing a photoshoot with flamboyant fashion-shoot energy
jokes.setup: Austin and Vanessa are having wedding/honeymoon photos taken
jokes.punchline: Austin takes over directing the shoot with over-the-top fashion photographer energy ('Fabulous, darling', 'Give it to me', 'You're an animal!', 'Show me the eye') — transforming a simple photo session into an absurd spectacle
jokes.explanation: Mike Myers commits fully to the fashion photographer bit, which is entertaining. It runs a bit long (nearly 90 seconds of transcript time) and the joke concept is familiar — but Austin's specific vocabulary and energy keep it going. 'Let's make a Vanessa sandwich' and 'The winged horn' are amusingly weird photographer-speak. Scores lower on economy because it stretches the concept.

jokes.text: Photographer: 'Never get up. I'm spent!'
jokes.setup: The photo shoot has concluded; the photographer gives a final reaction
jokes.punchline: 'I'm spent' — genuinely appropriate post-shoot exhaustion language that doubles perfectly as post-sexual climax language, consistent with the photo shoot's sustained innuendo
jokes.explanation: The button on the photo shoot double-entendre sequence. Works adequately as a punctuation mark but doesn't add new comedy — it's the fourth or fifth beat of the same joke structure. Economy is high (two words), but originality is low within this sequence.

jokes.text: Musical sequence: 'BBC One. BBC Two. BBC Three... BBC heaven.' — the song about wanting tea, sex, and BBC channels
jokes.setup: Austin performs an extended musical number with a list of BBC channels ascending to 'BBC heaven'
jokes.punchline: The song conflates mundane domestic requests (tea, BBC channels) with sexual overtures ('Make love to me') in an escalating, increasingly surreal list that culminates in 'BBC heaven' — treating British broadcasting with religious reverence
jokes.explanation: Entertainingly bizarre — the song is a Mike Myers construction that blends Austin's Britishness, his libido, and his absurdism. The escalation of BBC channels to 'heaven' is funny, and mixing 'make love to me' with 'make me tea' captures Austin perfectly. However, it repeats three full times in the transcript (through 85:05), which is excessive and hurts the economy score significantly. The concept is good; the execution is too long.

jokes.text: Second instance of Dr. Evil's revenge vow: 'I'm gonna get you, Austin Powers. It's frickin' freezing in here, Mr. Bigglesworth.'
jokes.setup: Intercut with Austin's BBC song, Dr. Evil is seen again in his rocket making the same complaint
jokes.punchline: The exact same line repeated — the temperature is still not fixed, the revenge monologue is still not complete, Dr. Evil is still cold
jokes.explanation: The callback to the same complaint works as a running gag — implying time has passed but Dr. Evil is still cold and still hasn't done anything about his revenge. Diminishing returns versus the first instance, but the structure of cutting between Austin's domestic silliness and Dr. Evil's perpetual cold gives it a fresh context. Gets a laugh as confirmation of the joke established earlier.

jokes.text: Second reprise of Dr. Evil in the rocket: 'I'm gonna get you, Austin Powers. It's frickin' freezing in here, Mr. Bigglesworth.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Evil appears again in his rocket, delivering the same villain threat and temperature complaint
jokes.punchline: The exact repetition of the joke (same words, same structure) works as a running gag — the second time it's funny BECAUSE it's identical, suggesting this is simply how Dr. Evil's villain speeches always end
jokes.explanation: The running gag payoff. The second identical repetition confirms this is Dr. Evil's standard operating procedure for villain speeches — he always deflates his own menace with the temperature complaint. The repetition is the joke: nothing has been learned, nothing has changed. High character integration because only Dr. Evil would do this. Originality is lower than the first instance by design — the structural repetition is the craft choice.
